Chapter 00

00 — Introduction: from problem to product

Why study PlumePilot?

Many programming courses teach a concept through examples deliberately designed to be simple:

fetch('/api/users')
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(users => console.log(users));

The example is useful for learning fetch, but it removes almost every problem that makes real-world software interesting:

  • who decides when the request should run?
  • what happens if the page changes in the meantime?
  • where do we store the result?
  • how much can we trust the data we received?
  • what happens if two parts of the application start the same operation?
  • how do we communicate the result to a UI that lives in another context?
  • what happens in Firefox if an API used in Chrome is not available in the same way?

PlumePilot contains all of these questions because it was not created as a teaching exercise. It grew out of concrete problems: moving through course activities, organizing study materials, creating quizzes that can be used offline, generating PDF and EPUB documents, observing changes in exam status, and providing all of this across three different browsers.

That makes the project a useful laboratory: the concepts are not artificially added to the explanation. They are already there because the problem made them necessary.

From a useful script to a small software system

At first, it is natural to think of a browser extension as “JavaScript running on top of a web page.”

That description quickly stops being sufficient.

The current PlumePilot includes, among other things:

  • an extension popup;
  • a background/service worker;
  • several groups of content scripts loaded at different times and in different contexts;
  • a bridge between the extension runtime and the page runtime;
  • persistent storage;
  • coordination of long-running operations;
  • separate generators for PDF, EPUB, and quizzes;
  • a floating menu injected into supported pages;
  • compatibility with Chrome, Edge, and Firefox;
  • a release build and validation process.

So the first important idea is:

A browser extension is not necessarily a single program. It can be a collection of small programs that live in different contexts and must coordinate with one another.

The manifest.json file tells the browser which pieces exist and when they should be loaded.

That will be the starting point of Chapter 1.

The recurring theme: where does the truth live?

Throughout this book, we will often return to one question:

What is our source of truth?

Suppose a chapter in the course UI shows 80%.

That number may be useful for understanding that something is probably still incomplete. But is it enough to decide exactly which activity should be opened?

Not necessarily.

We may have all of these at the same time:

visible DOM
    ↓
chapter percentage

API response
    ↓
lesson status

PlumePilot cache
    ↓
previously observed information

Three different sources, with different costs and different levels of reliability.

One of the most interesting steps in the development of the “first incomplete activity” search was precisely to stop treating a single source as a universal answer, and instead use some information as an index that tells us where to verify.

This distinction generalizes far beyond PlumePilot:

Information may not be reliable enough to be the final truth, while still being reliable enough to dramatically reduce the search space.

This is the kind of decision we also encounter in distributed systems, caches, search engines, and indexed databases.

The second theme: time

In synchronous textbook software, one thing happens after another.

In a browser, instead:

  • a page loads;
  • a content script starts;
  • an API response arrives;
  • the user opens or closes a chapter;
  • a video ends;
  • the popup is closed and reopened;
  • a timer expires;
  • a tab reloads;
  • the background may be suspended and later restarted.

Correctness therefore depends not only on what the code does, but also on when events happen.

That is why we will talk frequently about:

  • Promises;
  • events;
  • timeouts;
  • polling;
  • leases;
  • serialization;
  • race conditions;
  • cancellation;
  • idempotency.

The exam commission monitor is a good example. In the real code, bridge.js does not simply say “check the commission”: it first asks the background for the temporary right to run the check, receives a leaseId, performs the operation, and finally releases the lease.

That is not bureaucracy. It is concurrent coordination.

The third theme: boundaries

PlumePilot simultaneously lives next to three systems:

┌────────────────────┐
│ Browser / Extension│
│ API                │
└─────────┬──────────┘
          │
          │
┌─────────▼──────────┐
│ PlumePilot         │
└─────────┬──────────┘
          │
          │
┌─────────▼──────────┐
│ Multiversity       │
│ page + services    │
└────────────────────┘

Each boundary introduces different rules.

Page code can access the page's JavaScript objects, but not automatically the extension's privileged APIs. An isolated content script can use extension APIs, but it does not share the same JavaScript scope as the page. The background can coordinate the extension, but it cannot directly manipulate a tab's DOM.

Many of PlumePilot's architectural choices are consequences of these boundaries.

A useful analogy for backend developers

Without taking the analogy too literally, you can initially think of some components like this:

Popup / Floating UI
        ↓
   presentation
        ↓
Bridge / messaging
        ↓
 application boundary
        ↓
Background coordinator
        ↓
 state / orchestration

And the Multiversity page can be seen simultaneously as:

  • an external UI that we observe and modify;
  • an API client whose behavior we can understand by observing it;
  • a source of events;
  • a separate JavaScript environment.

The analogy with a service-oriented backend is not perfect, but it is useful: instead of direct function calls between every component, we often have messages and contracts.

What “finished” means for this book

Software is never permanently static. Browsers, platforms, and requirements change.

For us, “PlumePilot is finished” means something more practical:

  • the product has a mature functional scope;
  • the main architectural decisions are observable;
  • there is enough history of bugs, regressions, and improvements;
  • we can study the system without constantly chasing a new foundational feature.

That makes it possible to move from building the project to understanding it systematically.

How we will use the code

We will not comment on thousands of lines in order.

We will start from questions instead.

For example:

What happens when I click the PlumePilot icon?

or:

How can PlumePilot communicate with a function that exists in the page's JavaScript context?

or:

Why can a progress percentage speed up a search even though it is not 100% reliable?

Only then will we inspect the code needed to answer the question.

This is much closer to the way we actually read an unfamiliar real-world codebase.

Concepts to carry forward

Source of truth
The source we consider authoritative for a state or decision.

Boundary
The border between two components or runtimes that cannot directly share everything.

Message passing
Communication through messages instead of function calls within the same context.

Race condition
An error or unexpected behavior that depends on the timing or ordering of concurrent operations.

Idempotency
A property whereby repeating an operation does not cause additional unwanted effects.

Graceful degradation
The ability to keep working, perhaps with reduced functionality, when a capability is unavailable.

We will meet these concepts again in the code, not only in the glossary.

Before continuing

Keep one new question in mind:

If popup.js, background.js, bridge.js, and content.js are all JavaScript, why couldn't PlumePilot simply put everything into one file?

Chapter 1 starts from the answer.

01 · Anatomy of PlumePilot →
Chapter 01

01 — Anatomy of PlumePilot

What happens when the extension comes to life?

A browser extension does not start from main().

There is not necessarily a single entry point. Instead, the browser reads a special file, manifest.json, and from there discovers which components it must create, where they should live, and when they should run.

In our reference snapshot, the manifest begins like this:

{
  "manifest_version": 3,
  "name": "PlumePilot – Assistente per Multiversity",
  "version": "2.35.1"
}

manifest_version: 3 tells us that we are using the modern Chromium extension model and compatible WebExtensions.

But the truly interesting lines come shortly afterward.

1. The manifest as a map of the system

In PlumePilot's manifest.json we find four important families:

manifest.json
├── action
│   └── popup.html
│
├── background
│   └── background.js (+ support scripts)
│
├── content_scripts
│   ├── MAIN world
│   └── ISOLATED world
│
└── web_accessible_resources
    └── assets usable by supported pages

This is already our first architectural lesson:

The browser creates boundaries before our code even starts running.

We cannot understand PlumePilot by looking only at functions. We need to understand which runtime each function executes in.

2. The popup: an extension page

The manifest declares:

"action": {
  "default_title": "PlumePilot – Assistente per Multiversity",
  "default_popup": "popup.html"
}

When we click the PlumePilot icon, the browser opens popup.html, which loads the popup logic.

It is important to understand what the popup is not.

It is not an HTML element inserted into the Multiversity page.

It is a page that belongs to the extension, with its own document, its own lifecycle, and access to the APIs granted to the extension.

When the popup opens, popup.js rebuilds much of the visible state by reading chrome.storage.local:

chrome.storage.local.get(
  {
    enabled: true,
    stopAtTests: false,
    autoplaySkipCompletedVideos: false,
    themePreference: "system",
    menuSize: "medium",
    floatingMenuEnabled: true,
    commissionCheckEnabled: false,
    // ...
  },
  (result) => {
    // update the UI
  },
);

Real file: popup.js, approximately lines 1308–1375 in the reference snapshot.

Why rebuild the state?

Because the popup is ephemeral.

The user can open it, close it, and open it again. Treating the popup's JavaScript variables as the extension's persistent memory would be a poor design.

From a backend developer's perspective, you can think of the popup more as a view rebuilt from persistent state than as a central process that is always alive.

This anticipates a concept we will explore in the storage chapter:

The lifetime of a UI does not necessarily match the lifetime of the application's state.

3. The background: the coordinator that cannot see the DOM

In the manifest we find:

"background": {
  "scripts": [
    "achievements.js",
    "commission-state.js",
    "sound-settings.js",
    "whats-new.js",
    "background.js"
  ],
  "service_worker": "background.js"
}

This configuration supports the cross-browser source base.

In Chrome's Manifest V3 model, background.js is used as an extension service worker. Firefox supports the scripts form for background code. The same source base can therefore be transformed by the build process into the package best suited to each browser.

The conceptual role of the background matters more than the packaging detail:

The background coordinates activities that belong to the extension as a whole, not to a single page currently being displayed.

For example, near the end of background.js we find a real message dispatcher:

chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener((message, sender, sendResponse) => {
  let action = null;

  if (message?.type === "PEGASO_GET_OPERATION")
    action = reconcileOperationOwner();
  else if (message?.type === "PEGASO_START_EXPORT")
    action = startExport({ ...message, sourceTabId });
  else if (message?.type === "PEGASO_CANCEL_EXPORT")
    action = cancelExport(message);
  else if (message?.type === "PEGASO_COMMISSION_CHECK_CLAIM")
    action = claimCommissionCheck(sourceTabId, message.platformId);

  // ...

  action.then(sendResponse).catch(/* ... */);
  return true;
});

Real file: background.js, approximately lines 918–945.

This looks very similar to a backend router or controller:

message.type
    ↓
dispatcher
    ↓
handler
    ↓
asynchronous response

It is not HTTP, but the mental model is surprisingly similar.

So why doesn't the background do everything?

Because it does not live inside the page DOM.

If it needs to know which lessons are rendered, read a button on the page, or observe JavaScript state belonging to the site, it needs code that lives in the tab.

That is where content scripts enter the picture.

4. Content scripts: JavaScript inside a page, but not necessarily of the page

PlumePilot's manifest registers several groups of content_scripts.

One of them loads:

{
  "js": ["commission-interceptor.js"],
  "run_at": "document_start",
  "all_frames": false,
  "world": "MAIN"
}

Another loads:

{
  "js": [
    "commission-state.js",
    "sound-settings.js",
    "bridge.js"
  ],
  "run_at": "document_start",
  "all_frames": false
}

Here world is not specified, so the content script normally runs in the ISOLATED world.

This distinction is fundamental.

5. MAIN world and ISOLATED world

Imagine the Multiversity page as a room with the same table — the DOM — but two separate sets of JavaScript variables.

                 same DOM
                    │
        ┌───────────┴───────────┐
        │                       │
   MAIN world              ISOLATED world
        │                       │
 page code                content script
 + content.js             bridge.js
 + interceptor            floating-menu.js
        │                       │
        └──── window.postMessage ────┘

MAIN world

The code runs in the same JavaScript environment as the page.

This is useful when PlumePilot needs to observe or interact with behavior that belongs directly to the web application.

But there is a cost: that code does not automatically benefit from the isolation and privileged APIs normally available to content scripts.

ISOLATED world

The code shares the document and can therefore work with the DOM, but its JavaScript scope is separate from the page's scope.

In return, it is the appropriate place to use extension APIs such as chrome.storage and chrome.runtime.

This comment in content.js tells the architectural story almost better than the manifest:

// Receives the enabled/paused state from bridge.js, which runs in the
// extension's isolated world and therefore has access to chrome.storage.

Real file: content.js, approximately lines 248–249.

Immediately afterward, content.js listens for messages coming from the same window:

window.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
  if (event.source !== window) return;
  if (!event.data) return;

  // interpret bridge messages
});

So we have a deliberate pattern:

ISOLATED world
bridge.js
    │
    │ window.postMessage(...)
    ▼
MAIN world
content.js / interceptor

And in the opposite direction as well.

6. Why do we need bridge.js?

The name is not metaphorical. It really is a bridge.

Take the exam commission check.

bridge.js can talk to the background:

chrome.runtime.sendMessage({
  type: "PEGASO_COMMISSION_CHECK_CLAIM",
  platformId: PLATFORM_ID,
}, (response) => {
  // ...
});

But when it needs to ask code living in the MAIN world to perform an operation related to the page, it uses:

window.postMessage({
  type: COMMISSION_REQUEST,
  requestId: leaseId,
  expiresAt,
}, "*");

We can represent the flow like this:

This is message passing across boundaries.

If every component lived in the same scope, we could simply call a function:

requestCommissionData();

But these runtimes are separated. The message becomes the contract.

7. Popup → tab: another kind of message

The popup also needs to query the active tab directly.

In popup.js we find:

chrome.tabs.sendMessage(
  tabId,
  { type: "PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS_REQUEST" },
  { frameId: 0 },
  (response) => {
    if (chrome.runtime.lastError || !response?.status) return;
    renderCourseProgress(response.status);
  },
);

Here we are not using window.postMessage.

Why?

Because sender and recipient are not two JavaScript worlds in the same page: the sender is an extension page (the popup), while the recipient is a content script in the tab.

So we already have at least two different communication buses:

chrome.runtime / chrome.tabs messaging
    → between extension components

window.postMessage
    → between JavaScript worlds in the same page

This distinction will be at the heart of Chapter 2.

8. A more complete diagram

At this point we can build our first useful map of the architecture.

This is not yet the complete map of every feature, but it is enough to answer the opening question:

Why can't we put everything into a single file?

Because the responsibilities require different privileges, lifetimes, and execution environments.

9. run_at: when matters too

Content scripts are not all loaded at the same moment.

PlumePilot uses both:

"run_at": "document_start"

and:

"run_at": "document_idle"

document_start is useful when we need to be present very early in the page lifecycle. document_idle is appropriate when we can wait until the document is substantially ready.

For example, commission-interceptor.js is loaded in the MAIN world at document_start.

This suggests a general rule:

If you need to observe page behavior that may happen very early, arriving later means you may miss the event.

By contrast, a UI that depends on elements already present in the page can often wait until document_idle.

So the manifest specifies not only where code should run. It also specifies when it enters the life of the document.

10. all_frames: a page is not always a single document

Some script groups use:

"all_frames": true

This reminds us that a tab can contain iframes and therefore multiple documents.

It is easy to say “the script runs in the page,” but technically the better question is:

Which frame in the tab does it run in?

When the popup sends some requests to the tab, PlumePilot explicitly specifies:

{ frameId: 0 }

meaning the main frame.

It looks like a small detail, but it prevents ambiguity when the same extension may be loaded in multiple frames.

11. web_accessible_resources: extension assets visible to the page

The manifest also exposes some resources, such as Gaming-mode images, fonts, and audio.

Not everything included in an extension package must automatically be reachable by a web page.

web_accessible_resources explicitly declares which files can be requested from contexts that match the declared patterns.

This is another example of the least privilege principle:

expose what is needed, not the entire package.

The same principle will return when we discuss permissions and host_permissions.

12. Permissions: what PlumePilot can do is not implicit

In the current snapshot, the manifest declares:

"permissions": ["storage"]

along with host_permissions for hosts needed to manage materials and resources.

Extension APIs are explicit capabilities. This differs from an ordinary web page, where code already runs within the site's origin security model.

When we mentally design a feature, a good question will always be:

Which context should this function live in, and what is the minimum privilege it needs?

That question often determines the architecture before it determines the code.

13. A concrete case: the popup wants to show progress

Let us finally follow a small end-to-end path.

Step 1 — the user opens the popup

The browser creates popup.html and runs popup.js.

Step 2 — the popup rebuilds persistent preferences

popup.js
    ↓
chrome.storage.local.get(...)
    ↓
UI rendering

Step 3 — it identifies the active tab

In the code we find:

chrome.tabs.query({ active: true, currentWindow: true }, ...)

Step 4 — it requests course state

popup
  │
  │ PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS_REQUEST
  ▼
content script in the tab

through chrome.tabs.sendMessage.

Step 5 — it receives the state and renders it

renderCourseProgress(response.status);

Step 6 — it keeps listening

The popup also registers:

chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener(...)

so it can update itself when new state arrives while it is open.

The popup therefore does not “own” progress. It displays it.

This is an excellent example of separating state from presentation.

14. For backend developers: three analogies

chrome.runtime.onMessage as an internal router

You can think of message.type values as logical endpoints:

PEGASO_START_EXPORT
PEGASO_CANCEL_EXPORT
PEGASO_GET_OPERATION
...

They are not URLs, but they identify commands and requests.

The background as an application service

It coordinates operations, storage, and ownership without knowing the visual details of the DOM.

The bridge as an adapter

It translates communication and capabilities between two incompatible environments:

Extension APIs ⇄ bridge ⇄ Page runtime

In software architecture, we would often call a component like this an adapter or gateway.

15. An important architectural note: a large file does not automatically mean bad architecture

The current snapshot contains several very large files, including content.js, floating-menu.js, and popup.js.

It is easy to look only at size and conclude that the system is monolithic.

But there are two different levels:

  1. physical modularity — how we divide code into files;
  2. runtime modularity — which responsibilities live in separate processes/contexts.

PlumePilot has room for greater physical modularity, a topic we will revisit in the final chapter. But it already has real runtime boundaries imposed and used by the WebExtensions architecture.

It is important not to confuse the two.

16. What we learned from manifest.json alone

Without yet studying autoplay, APIs, or EPUB, we already know that PlumePilot:

  • uses Manifest V3;
  • has a popup UI separate from the page;
  • has a background coordinator;
  • executes code in both the MAIN and ISOLATED worlds;
  • uses different timings (document_start / document_idle);
  • explicitly accounts for different frames;
  • exposes only selected resources to the page;
  • requests capabilities through declared permissions;
  • must use messaging to cross boundaries.

The manifest is therefore much more than “store metadata.”

It is a declarative map of the runtime architecture.

Concepts to carry forward

Execution context

The environment in which a piece of code runs: which globals it sees, which APIs it can use, and what lifetime it has.

MAIN world

The JavaScript context shared with the web page.

ISOLATED world

A separate context used by content scripts that shares the DOM but not the page's JavaScript scope.

Extension page

An HTML page that belongs to the extension, such as the popup.

Background / service worker

A component dedicated to handling events and operations that do not belong to a single page.

Message passing

Communication between separated components through serializable messages.

Adapter / bridge

A component that translates between different interfaces or environments.

Least privilege

Granting and exposing only the capabilities that are actually needed.

Small thought exercise

Before reading the next chapter, try to classify these operations:

  1. saving the themePreference preference;
  2. reading a JavaScript value that belongs to the Multiversity page;
  3. displaying that value in the popup;
  4. coordinating an export that must survive the popup being closed;
  5. updating an element in the course DOM.

For each one, ask yourself:

Where should it live?
Popup?
Background?
MAIN world?
ISOLATED world?

Not all of them have only one possible answer. The point is to start reasoning in terms of boundaries and responsibilities.

In the next chapter

Now we know who the components are.

The next question is:

How do they communicate without turning the extension into an impossible-to-follow network of messages?

We will follow a real message from the UI to the background, from the tab to the bridge, and from the bridge to the MAIN world. We will look at callbacks, Promises, sendResponse, asynchronous listener lifetimes, window.postMessage, and the first real concurrency problems.

Chapter 02

02 — Contexts and messaging

Making separate worlds communicate

In the previous chapter we saw that PlumePilot does not live inside a single JavaScript environment.

The popup, background, isolated content scripts, MAIN-world scripts, and builder pages are separate components. They belong to the same extension, but they do not automatically share memory, global scope, or lifecycle.

In an ordinary function, we can write:

const result = calculateSomething(input);

Across extension contexts, the interaction looks more like this:

component A
    │
    │  { type: "DO_SOMETHING", ... }
    ▼
boundary
    │
    ▼
component B
    │
    │  { accepted: true, ... }
    ▼
component A

Component A does not directly invoke one of B's private functions. Instead it sends a message describing what it wants to accomplish. This is message passing, one of the most useful concepts for understanding PlumePilot.

1. From function calls to contracts

When two pieces of code share a scope, the contract can simply be a function signature:

startExport(format, tabId);

Across a boundary, the contract becomes serializable data:

{
  type: "PEGASO_START_EXPORT",
  format: "materials",
  sourceTabId: tabId,
  requestSource: "toolbar-popup"
}

The object carries a request, not executable behavior. Its type field plays a role similar to an HTTP route such as POST /exports/start. The recipient uses it to choose the handler.

In background.js, the dispatcher follows this pattern:

chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener((message, sender, sendResponse) => {
  let action = null;

  if (message?.type === "PEGASO_GET_OPERATION")
    action = reconcileOperationOwner();
  else if (message?.type === "PEGASO_START_EXPORT")
    action = startExport({ ...message, sourceTabId });
  else if (message?.type === "PEGASO_CANCEL_EXPORT")
    action = cancelExport(message);

  // ...
});

Source: background.js, message dispatcher.

message.type
     │
     ├── PEGASO_START_EXPORT  → startExport()
     ├── PEGASO_CANCEL_EXPORT → cancelExport()
     └── PEGASO_GET_OPERATION → reconcileOperationOwner()

A concept to remember

Crossing a boundary does not merely mean "calling a function somewhere else." It means defining a protocol, even when that protocol is entirely internal to an application.

2. PlumePilot's three main communication channels

Three mechanisms appear repeatedly:

1. chrome.runtime.sendMessage()
2. chrome.tabs.sendMessage()
3. window.postMessage()

They may look similar, but they solve different problems.

chrome.runtime.sendMessage()

This sends a message within the extension runtime, typically to the background coordinator:

chrome.runtime.sendMessage(message, (response) => {
  // use the response
});

Use it when the destination is an extension component rather than a content script in a particular tab.

chrome.tabs.sendMessage()

This addresses the content scripts in a specific browser tab:

chrome.tabs.sendMessage(
  tabId,
  { type: "PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS_REQUEST" },
  { frameId: 0 },
  callback,
);

Notice the addressing information: the tab ID, and in this case the top frame.

window.postMessage()

This is a standard Web API, not an extension-specific one. PlumePilot uses it to bridge the ISOLATED and MAIN worlds, which share the page's window but not the same JavaScript scope.

// bridge.js
window.postMessage(
  { type: "PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS_REQUEST" },
  "*",
);
// content.js
window.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
  if (event.source !== window) return;
  if (!event.data) return;

  if (event.data.type === "PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS_REQUEST") {
    // ...
  }
});

The page's window acts as a local message channel.

3. A mental map of the channels

                         EXTENSION

 popup / builder                       background
      │                                    ▲
      │ chrome.runtime.sendMessage         │
      └────────────────────────────────────┘

 background / popup
      │
      │ chrome.tabs.sendMessage(tabId)
      ▼
 bridge.js / isolated content script
      │
      │ window.postMessage
      ▼
 content.js / MAIN world
      │
      ▼
 Multiversity page

Messages may travel back in the opposite direction as well. The important question is: which boundary does this message need to cross?

When reading the code, first ask: "Which context am I in, and which context am I trying to reach?"

Part I — A simple flow

4. Real example: the popup requests course progress

When the popup opens, it needs information about the current course. In popup.js:

chrome.tabs.sendMessage(
  tabId,
  { type: "PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS_REQUEST" },
  { frameId: 0 },
  (response) => {
    if (chrome.runtime.lastError || !response?.status) return;
    renderCourseProgress(response.status);
  },
);

Source: popup.js L1392–L1399.

The popup knows the active tab ID and addresses that tab's isolated content script, bridge.js. Its listener handles the request approximately as follows:

if (message?.type === "PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS_REQUEST") {
  window.postMessage(
    { type: "PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS_REQUEST" },
    "*",
  );

  sendResponse({
    accepted: true,
    status: courseProgressStatus,
  });

  return;
}

Source: bridge.js L368–L371.

Two things happen:

  1. The bridge immediately returns the last known progress status.
  2. At the same time, it requests a refresh from the MAIN world.

These are separate operations with different timing guarantees.

5. Immediate response, later update

A naive implementation might make the popup wait for a complete recalculation:

popup → calculate everything → wait → respond

PlumePilot instead uses a more reactive pattern:

popup
  ├── receives last known snapshot immediately
  └── triggers a refresh in MAIN
                      │
                      ▼
                new status
                      │
                      ▼
                pushed update

The bridge's courseProgressStatus is a snapshot cache: useful for a responsive interface, even if a fresher value is still being calculated.

This introduces eventual consistency

For a short period, two components may hold different snapshots. They converge as updates propagate. That does not automatically mean something is broken; consistency is obtained through messages rather than synchronously shared memory.

This model appears throughout distributed systems, reactive interfaces, and event-driven applications. PlumePilot gives us a compact example we can inspect directly.

6. Crossing the ISOLATED → MAIN boundary

The bridge first crosses from the extension's isolated context into the page's JavaScript world:

window.postMessage(
  { type: "PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS_REQUEST" },
  "*",
);

After that request, content.js in the MAIN world receives it:

if (event.data.type === "PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS_REQUEST") {
  scheduleCourseProgressInitialization(0);
  publishCourseProgressStatus();
  return;
}

Source: content.js L423–L426.

The MAIN world computes or publishes its own state:

window.postMessage({
  type: "PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS",
  status: {
    courseCode: state.courseCode,
    available: percent !== null && state.chapterCount > 0,
    percent,
    chapterCount: state.chapterCount,
    knownChapters: courseProgressChapters.size,
    exact: exactAvailable,
    // ...
  },
}, "*");

Source: content.js L4478–L4500.

Now the message travels in the opposite direction, returning from the page runtime to the extension bridge:

content.js (MAIN)
    │ window.postMessage
    ▼
bridge.js (ISOLATED)

The crucial point is that the messaging boundary separates two JavaScript worlds even though both can observe the same tab's document.

7. The bridge as an adapter

The bridge does not blindly forward the returned payload. It normalizes it first:

courseProgressStatus = courseCode ? {
  platformId: PLATFORM_ID,
  courseCode,
  available: source.available === true && Number.isFinite(percent),
  percent: Number.isFinite(percent)
    ? Math.max(0, Math.min(100, Math.floor(percent)))
    : null,
  chapterCount: Math.max(0, Math.floor(Number(source.chapterCount) || 0)),
  knownChapters: Math.max(0, Math.floor(Number(source.knownChapters) || 0)),
  exact: source.exact === true,
  updatedByStudyWing: source.updatedByStudyWing === true,
  message: safeText(source.message, 160) || "",
} : null;

Then it publishes the normalized state to the extension runtime:

chrome.runtime.sendMessage({
  type: "PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS",
  status: courseProgressStatus,
});

Source: bridge.js L513–L534.

The word bridge is appropriate, but adapter is equally important:

MAIN-world payload
      ↓
validation and normalization
      ↓
extension-runtime payload

The adapter applies explicit defenses such as Number.isFinite(percent), Math.max(...), Math.min(...), and safeText(...) before data reaches another context. In other words, it decides the shape and range of acceptable values, not merely where to forward them.

General principle

A boundary is a natural place to validate, normalize, reduce, reject, or translate data. The same principle motivates DTOs, serializers, and adapters in backend architectures.

8. The popup receives the pushed update

The initial reply is not the popup's only source of information:

chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener((message, sender) => {
  if (
    message?.type === "PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS" &&
    sender?.tab?.id === activeCourseTabId
  ) {
    renderCourseProgress(message.status || null);
  }
});

Source: popup.js L1402–L1409.

The sender check matters. Without it, progress events from tab B might update the UI for course A.

The explicit sender?.tab?.id === activeCourseTabId check prevents an unrelated course tab from overwriting the displayed progress. A message system needs to ask not only what type of message is this?, but also who sent it?

9. The entire progress flow

We have request, immediate response, asynchronous refresh, pushed update, snapshot cache, and sender validation—all in one relatively small workflow.

Part II — Asynchronous request/response

10. sendResponse() and the problem of time

Consider the background listener:

chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener((message, sender, sendResponse) => {
  let action = null;

  // ... select the action ...

  action
    .then(sendResponse)
    .catch((error) => {
      sendResponse({ accepted: false, reason: error.message });
    });

  return true;
});

Why return true?

With a synchronous response, the handler can call sendResponse before it finishes:

chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener((message, sender, sendResponse) => {
  sendResponse({ accepted: true });
});

With an asynchronous response, the Promise may settle after the listener has returned:

chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener((message, sender, sendResponse) => {
  doSomethingAsync().then((result) => {
    sendResponse(result);
  });

  return true;
});

In this callback-based messaging model, return true keeps the response channel available for the later callback.

request → handler → asynchronous work starts
                      ↓
                 listener returns
                      ↓
            Promise settles later
                      ↓
                  sendResponse

Without the required signal, the channel may already have closed when the response is attempted.

Backend analogy

Think of a route that needs a database query before producing its response. The analogy is imperfect—the extension runtime manages the callback channel—but the same timing question arises: is the response produced before or after the initial handler returns?

11. Why PlumePilot wraps callbacks in Promises

The popup defines this adapter around the callback-oriented runtime API:

function runtimeMessage(message) {
  return new Promise((resolve) =>
    chrome.runtime.sendMessage(message, (response) =>
      resolve(
        chrome.runtime.lastError
          ? { accepted: false, reason: chrome.runtime.lastError.message }
          : response,
      ),
    ),
  );
}

Source: popup.js L1296–L1306.

The caller can then write:

const response = await runtimeMessage({
  type: "PEGASO_START_EXPORT",
  // ...
});

instead of nesting callbacks. The helper has two responsibilities:

  1. It converts a callback-based browser API into a Promise.
  2. It converts chrome.runtime.lastError into a regular application response.

The second detail is especially important. Rather than making every caller remember:

if (chrome.runtime.lastError) {
  // ...
}

the helper provides one consistent result shape:

{
  accepted: false,
  reason: "..."
}

A small asynchronous adapter

We can describe the actual boundary as:

Browser API
(callback + runtime.lastError)
          │
          ▼
runtimeMessage()
          │
          ▼
PlumePilot internal API
(Promise + accepted/reason)

The adapter in this historical snapshot resolves with an error-shaped value; it does not reject the Promise for chrome.runtime.lastError. The caller is responsible for checking the returned accepted field.

Boundaries are natural places to translate one interface into another.

Part III — A long-running workflow

12. Real example: exporting course materials

The progress request is short. Exporting course materials is different: collection can take time, the popup may close, and a separate builder page must eventually produce a file.

The workflow crosses multiple contexts and uses its own operation identity.

13. Step 1 — The popup sends a command

When the user starts material collection:

const response = await runtimeMessage({
  type: "PEGASO_START_EXPORT",
  format: "materials",
  sourceTabId: tabId,
  requestSource: "toolbar-popup",
});

Source: popup.js L2112–L2133.

This is a command: an intention to start something.

Command

START_EXPORT
CANCEL_EXPORT
FIND_FIRST_INCOMPLETE

Event

An event describes something that already happened:

COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS
COURSE_MATERIALS_COLLECTED
EXPORT_COLLECTION_FAILED

The code does not implement formal CQRS or event sourcing, but the conceptual distinction helps us trace messages.

14. Step 2 — The background acquires the operation

The dispatcher routes the command to startExport(), which first attempts to acquire ownership:

const result = await acquire(format, message.sourceTabId);
if (!result.accepted) return result;

Source: background.js L700–L719.

Collection does not start immediately. The background first checks whether the operation may proceed, preventing incompatible workflows from running concurrently.

This is why a coordinator with a global view is useful: no individual course tab necessarily knows every operation in progress.

15. Step 3 — An operationId is created

The acquired operation has an ID:

result.operation.id

It is carried into messages sent to the course tab:

const response = await sendTabMessage(message.sourceTabId, {
  type: "PEGASO_COLLECT_COURSE_MATERIALS",
  format,
  operationId: result.operation.id,
});

Without an identifier, a sequence of messages might look like:

START
STATUS 25%
STATUS 80%
COMPLETE

But which export do these updates describe?

operationId = 9f2...

START     9f2...
STATUS    9f2...
STATUS    9f2...
COMPLETE  9f2...

The identifier acts as a correlation ID, a fundamental pattern in asynchronous jobs, queues, tracing, and distributed systems.

16. Step 4 — The background addresses a specific tab

The helper used for tab messaging is shaped like this:

function sendTabMessage(tabId, message) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
    chrome.tabs.sendMessage(
      tabId,
      message,
      { frameId: 0 },
      (response) =>
        chrome.runtime.lastError
          ? reject(new Error(chrome.runtime.lastError.message))
          : resolve(response),
    ),
  );
}

Source: background.js L677–L683.

tabId and frameId: 0 are addresses. This is not a broadcast to every tab; it is a request to a specific content-script destination.

17. Step 5 — The bridge deduplicates before forwarding

The isolated bridge checks the operation ID:

if (message?.type === "PEGASO_COLLECT_COURSE_MATERIALS") {
  const operationId = exportOperationId(message.operationId);

  if (!operationId) {
    sendResponse({
      accepted: false,
      reason: "Identificativo operazione mancante.",
    });
    return;
  }

  if (requestedExportOperationIds.has(operationId)) {
    sendResponse({ accepted: true, duplicate: true });
    return;
  }

  rememberExportOperation(requestedExportOperationIds, operationId);

  window.postMessage({
    type: "PEGASO_COLLECT_COURSE_MATERIALS_REQUEST",
    format: message.format,
    operationId,
  }, "*");

  sendResponse({ accepted: true, duplicate: false });
}

Source: bridge.js L373–L390.

The error message is left in Italian because it comes from the actual code snapshot, not from a translated UI.

True idempotency versus deduplication

Setting a preference to the same value repeatedly is naturally idempotent:

SET theme = dark
SET theme = dark
SET theme = dark

Collecting all course materials is expensive. PlumePilot instead asks whether the same operationId has already been observed.

This provides a useful form of duplicate suppression within the lifetime of the component that remembers the ID. It is not a blanket guarantee of exactly-once execution or permanent idempotency. We should never attribute stronger guarantees to the code than it really provides.

18. Step 6 — Collection begins in the MAIN world

The bridge posts the command into the MAIN world. content.js checks the ID again before the actual side effect:

if (event.data.type === "PEGASO_COLLECT_COURSE_MATERIALS_REQUEST") {
  const operationId = /* normalization */;

  if (!operationId) return;

  if (handledExportOperationIds.has(operationId)) {
    return;
  }

  rememberHandledExportOperation(operationId);

  void collectCourseMaterials(format, operationId).finally(() => {
    // completion logging
  });

  return;
}

Source: content.js L287–L311.

Why deduplicate again? Because the layers defend different boundaries:

  • bridge.js protects the transfer from the extension runtime into MAIN.
  • content.js protects the actual collection side effect.

This is defence in depth for reliability, not only for security.

19. Why void collectCourseMaterials(...) instead of await?

void collectCourseMaterials(format, operationId).finally(...);

The message handler does not await the entire collection. Starting the workflow is a short operation; completing it may take much longer.

short request/response
          ≠
long asynchronous workflow

Instead of holding a message response open for the entire job, PlumePilot sends subsequent events:

COMMAND: start
EVENT:   status updated
EVENT:   status updated
EVENT:   completed

The backend analogy is familiar:

POST /exports
→ 202 Accepted + jobId

GET /jobs/:id
or pushed events

20. Step 7 — Status updates travel back up the chain

During collection, the MAIN world publishes progress:

window.postMessage(
  {
    type: "PEGASO_EXPORT_COLLECTION_STATUS",
    operationId,
    message,
  },
  "*",
);

Source: content.js L2388–L2401.

The bridge converts it into an extension-runtime update:

chrome.runtime.sendMessage({
  type: "PEGASO_UPDATE_OPERATION",
  operationId,
  patch: { message: event.data.message },
});

Source: bridge.js L584–L588.

content.js
    ↓ status event
bridge.js
    ↓ operation update
background
    ↓
central operation state

The user may close the popup while collection continues. When the popup opens again, it can reconstruct its UI from the operation state.

The UI does not own the job. The UI observes the job.

21. Step 8 — Collection ends with an event

When the payload is ready, the MAIN world publishes PEGASO_COURSE_MATERIALS_COLLECTED.

The bridge checks a different set for terminal events:

if (terminalExportOperationIds.has(operationId)) {
  return;
}

rememberExportOperation(
  terminalExportOperationIds,
  operationId,
);

Then:

chrome.runtime.sendMessage({
  type: "PEGASO_OPEN_EXPORT_BUILDER",
  format: event.data.format,
  operationId,
  payload: event.data.payload,
});

Source: bridge.js L550–L570.

The workflow has two distinct moments worth protecting:

START    → do not start twice
COMPLETE → do not finalize twice

Duplicate completion events must not open duplicate builder pages.

22. Step 9 — The background opens the builder only once

The background checks that finalization is not already in progress:

if (
  operation.phase === "building" ||
  operation.jobKey ||
  Number.isInteger(operation.builderTabId)
) {
  return {
    accepted: true,
    duplicate: true,
    operation,
  };
}

Source: background.js L784–L850.

It creates a new jobId, stores the payload, and opens a builder page:

const jobId = crypto.randomUUID();
const storageKey = `pegasoExportJob:${jobId}`;

await storageSet({
  [storageKey]: {
    ...message.payload,
    format,
    operationId: operation.id,
    courseTabId: operation.sourceTabId,
  },
});

chrome.tabs.create({
  url: chrome.runtime.getURL(`${builderPage}?job=${jobId}`),
});

The URL carries only a small reference, ?job=<jobId>. The builder retrieves the larger payload from storage.

This is the familiar backend pattern:

small identifier → lookup of large state

23. The complete export workflow

We are not merely looking at a script that clicks buttons; this is a small event-driven system.

Part IV — Protocol reliability

24. accepted does not mean completed

A message response such as:

{ accepted: true }

usually means the request was accepted for further handling. For example, the bridge actually replies:

sendResponse({ accepted: true, duplicate: false });

The duplicate field distinguishes a newly accepted request from a repeated one that is acknowledged without starting a second collection. It does not mean the course materials have already been generated.

accepted ≠ completed

As with HTTP 202 Accepted, the response is about admission into a workflow, not necessarily about the workflow's final result.

25. Three classes of messages

A useful mental classification is:

A. Query

A request for information:

PEGASO_GET_OPERATION
PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS_REQUEST
PEGASO_CHAPTER_LIMIT_STATUS_REQUEST

B. Command

An intention to perform an action:

PEGASO_START_EXPORT
PEGASO_CANCEL_EXPORT
PEGASO_FIND_FIRST_INCOMPLETE_COMMAND

C. Event

A statement about something that happened:

PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS
PEGASO_COURSE_MATERIALS_COLLECTED
PEGASO_EXPORT_COLLECTION_FAILED

This is a reading aid, not a taxonomy formally enforced by the browser or codebase.

26. Fire-and-forget versus request/response

Not every message requires an awaited application response.

Request/response

chrome.runtime.sendMessage(message, (response) => {
  // the reply matters to the caller
});

Fire-and-forget

chrome.runtime.sendMessage({
  type: "PEGASO_UPDATE_OPERATION",
  operationId,
  patch: { message },
});

The sender can continue without waiting for a domain result. This reduces coupling, but it changes error handling: a lost update must not silently make the overall workflow impossible to understand.

Ask whether the sender needs proof that the recipient completed the action, or merely needs to publish the information.

27. Transport errors versus application errors

A transport/runtime error may be exposed through:

chrome.runtime.lastError

The target tab might have been closed, the content script might be unavailable, or the response channel might have failed.

An application error means the message arrived but the operation was rejected:

{
  accepted: false,
  reason: "Scheda del corso non disponibile."
}

Again, the Italian string is preserved from the code example. The conceptual distinction is analogous to:

network/transport failure
           ≠
successfully delivered domain error

28. Why runtime.lastError is checked so frequently

chrome.tabs.sendMessage(tabId, message, (response) => {
  if (chrome.runtime.lastError) {
    // handle delivery error
    return;
  }

  // use response
});

In callback-style Chrome APIs, asynchronous runtime failures may be reported through chrome.runtime.lastError. If it is ignored, a result such as:

response === undefined

might be mistaken for a meaningful domain response even though the message never reached its destination.

Promise wrappers help turn this API-specific pattern into consistent handling for the rest of the code.

29. Messages must be serializable

Messaging does not share JavaScript object identity or the same heap.

It is inappropriate to design a message that expects a callback or DOM node to be directly usable in the recipient:

{
  callback: () => doSomething(),
  domNode: document.querySelector("video")
}

Instead, send data:

{
  type: "PEGASO_UPDATE_OPERATION",
  operationId: "...",
  patch: {
    phase: "building",
    message: "Preparazione in corso…"
  }
}

Serializable contracts force boundaries to become explicit. That constraint is often an architectural advantage.

Part V — window.postMessage() and the trust boundary

30. Sharing window does not mean sharing trust

A message listener may check:

if (event.source !== window || !event.data) return;

This verifies that the event came from the expected window object, but it is not cryptographic authentication. Page JavaScript can also post messages on the same window.

Treat MAIN ↔︎ ISOLATED as a trust boundary:

  • Accept only the message types you need.
  • Validate identifiers, values, and payload shapes.
  • Avoid moving secrets between contexts unnecessarily.
  • Normalize information before sending it into the more privileged extension runtime.

Examples of defensive helpers in PlumePilot include safeText(...), exportOperationId(...), Number.isFinite(...), and Array.isArray(...).

General lesson

Prefer a narrow bridge with a handful of explicit, validated commands over a general "execute whatever the other side requests" interface.

The same principle applies to iframes, workers, plugin systems, and backend APIs.

31. Why "*" as targetOrigin does not mean "send this to the Internet"

window.postMessage(message, "*");

Here, "*" does not restrict the target origin, but the target is still the page's own window. It does not broadcast the message to arbitrary websites.

Nevertheless, JavaScript running in the page may be able to observe or post messages on that channel. The payload should not be treated as secret. For communications between different windows or origins, strict origin verification becomes even more important.

Part VI — Concurrency hidden inside messages

32. Two valid messages may still cause a bug

Imagine two valid commands:

A: START_EXPORT
B: CANCEL_EXPORT

What if they arrive almost simultaneously?

Or imagine:

A: STATUS 40%
B: COMPLETE
C: STATUS 50%  ← arrives late

The problem is not an invalid payload. It is ordering and timing.

That is why PlumePilot uses operation IDs, phases, deduplication sets, serialized background operations, and guards around terminal events. We will explore these patterns further in the asynchrony chapter.

In a message-driven system, time and ordering are part of the design.

33. Terminal state is special

if (terminalExportOperationIds.has(operationId)) {
  return;
}

Once a workflow has ended, a late or duplicate message should not reopen it.

idle
  ↓
collecting
  ↓
building
  ↓
completed / released

A message can be syntactically valid yet invalid for the current lifecycle phase. This is our first glimpse of why explicit state machines are helpful.

Part VII — Startup and synchronization

34. A listener may be registered too late

A comment in content.js reveals a real startup-ordering issue:

// bridge.js may have sent its startup state before this document-idle
// listener existed. Request an explicit synchronization after subscribing.
window.postMessage({ type: "PEGASO_AUTONEXT_STATE_REQUEST" }, "*");

Source: content.js L557–L559.

Recall the injection timing:

bridge.js  → document_start
content.js → document_idle

This can happen:

bridge loads
    ↓
bridge publishes startup state
    ↓
content.js has not registered its listener yet
    ↓
message is lost

postMessage is not a persistent queue. It cannot retroactively deliver an event that no suitable listener was ready to process.

PlumePilot fixes the ordering problem by:

  1. Registering the listener.
  2. Explicitly requesting current state.
  3. Receiving a fresh publication from the bridge.

This is a handshake, or explicit synchronization.

Important concept

Events tell you "something changed." New subscribers also need a way to ask "what is the state right now?"

35. Snapshot plus events: a recurring pattern

QUERY
  ↓
current snapshot

EVENT
  ↓
future changes

The snapshot brings a newly started or reopened component up to date. Events keep it informed afterward.

Backend analogies include an initial GET /resource followed by a WebSocket or SSE subscription, or a database query followed by change notifications.

The implementations differ, but the architectural problem is the same.

Part VIII — How to read PlumePilot's messaging

36. A practical reverse-engineering method

When you encounter a message.type, reconstruct the path in four steps.

1. Find its producer

Search for:

{ type: "MESSAGE_NAME" }

Ask: who sends it?

2. Find its consumer

Search for:

message?.type === "MESSAGE_NAME"

or:

event.data.type === "MESSAGE_NAME"

Ask: who receives it?

3. Identify the channel

Is the producer calling runtime.sendMessage, tabs.sendMessage, or window.postMessage? That reveals the boundary.

4. Find the response or next event

REQUEST → STATUS
START   → UPDATE → COMPLETE

Once you can trace producers, recipients, channels, and follow-up events, you have reconstructed the protocol.

37. A table of the main boundaries

From To Typical mechanism Example
Popup Background runtime.sendMessage Start export
Builder Background runtime.sendMessage Update/release operation
Background Content script tabs.sendMessage Collect materials
Popup Content script tabs.sendMessage Request course progress
ISOLATED MAIN window.postMessage Collection command
MAIN ISOLATED window.postMessage Status/completion
Bridge Popup/extension runtime runtime.sendMessage Updated progress

This is almost a dependency map of PlumePilot's runtime architecture.

Part IX — What could we have done differently?

38. A single message bus?

We could create one abstraction:

bus.send("START_EXPORT", payload);

It might hide whether the implementation calls runtime.sendMessage, tabs.sendMessage, or postMessage.

Benefit

Calling code could become more uniform.

Cost

It could hide important architecture: where is this message going, which boundary does it cross, and what capabilities does the receiver have?

A useful abstraction might centralize error handling and contracts while keeping destinations explicit, rather than hiding every difference.

39. A centralized registry of message types?

Today, many message names are string literals scattered across the codebase:

"PEGASO_START_EXPORT"
"PEGASO_UPDATE_OPERATION"
"PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS"

One possible evolution would be:

const Messages = Object.freeze({
  START_EXPORT: "PEGASO_START_EXPORT",
  UPDATE_OPERATION: "PEGASO_UPDATE_OPERATION",
  COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS: "PEGASO_COURSE_PROGRESS_STATUS",
});

TypeScript could also associate payload types with each message.

What would we gain?

Fewer typos, easier refactoring, visible contracts, and potential type checking.

What would it cost?

More infrastructure, a shared module available in several execution contexts, and potentially limited value for very small messages.

The current approach is not automatically wrong. This is the kind of trade-off we will revisit in the architectural retrospective.

40. A versioned protocol?

Components in one extension package normally update together. PlumePilot therefore does not need every message to carry a field such as:

protocolVersion: 3

In a system where senders and receivers deploy independently, versioned contracts would become much more important.

The amount of protocol infrastructure you need depends partly on how your components are distributed and released.

Part X — Connections to backend development

41. A shared vocabulary

Browser extension Backend/distributed-system analogy
message.type Route, event name, or command name
runtime.onMessage Dispatcher/controller
sendResponse() Response handler
operationId Job ID/correlation ID
accepted: true Accepted request/202 Accepted
runtime.lastError Transport/runtime failure
accepted: false Domain/application failure
window.postMessage Local message bus / IPC-like boundary
tabs.sendMessage(tabId) Addressing one particular instance
Snapshot + events Initial query + subscription
Deduplication Duplicate suppression/idempotency key

These are analogies, not exact equivalences. A browser extension is not a distributed cluster, and postMessage is not Kafka. But the underlying questions are related: separated components, asynchronous delivery, partial failures, timing, correlation, duplicate handling, and non-shared state.

Part XI — Small exercises

42. Exercise 1 — Choose the channel

Imagine implementing these features.

A. The popup asks the background whether an export is active

Use runtime.sendMessage: the recipient is the extension-wide coordinator.

B. The background asks tab 37 to stop collecting materials

Use tabs.sendMessage(37, ...): this addresses a particular content script.

C. content.js in MAIN asks the bridge to read a stored preference

Use window.postMessage to cross MAIN → ISOLATED; the bridge then uses the appropriate extension APIs.

43. Exercise 2 — Find the bug

chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener((message, sender, sendResponse) => {
  fetchSomething().then((result) => {
    sendResponse(result);
  });
});

What is missing from the callback-based pattern used by PlumePilot?

return true;

Without it, the asynchronous response channel may close before fetchSomething() completes.

44. Exercise 3 — Query, command, or event?

PEGASO_GET_OPERATION         → query
PEGASO_CANCEL_EXPORT        → command
PEGASO_EXPORT_COLLECTION_FAILED → event

The browser does not demand this classification. It is a way for us to reason more clearly.

45. Exercise 4 — Why do we need operationId?

Suppose exports A and B are started close together. A message arrives saying only "collection completed."

Without an operation identity, we cannot tell which export it refers to. With operationId: A, the message is unambiguous.

46. Exercise 5 — An event lost during startup

bridge.js: document_start
content.js: document_idle

If the bridge publishes startup state only once, content.js may not receive it because its listener does not exist yet.

A robust strategy is:

subscribe → request current snapshot

That is exactly the purpose served by PEGASO_AUTONEXT_STATE_REQUEST.

Part XII — Concepts to carry forward

47. Message passing

Communicating through messages instead of directly sharing functions and memory.

48. Protocol

The set of message shapes, names, and expectations that allow senders and receivers to understand one another. In PlumePilot it largely consists of objects with a type and associated payload.

49. Dispatcher

A component that routes incoming messages to the appropriate handler. The background's runtime.onMessage listener is an example.

50. Command

A message expressing an intention to perform an action.

51. Event

A message describing something that has happened.

52. Query

A message primarily requesting information, not requesting a state change.

53. Correlation ID

An identifier linking multiple messages to one logical workflow. operationId is our central example.

54. Deduplication

Recognizing and suppressing a repeated request or event that has already been processed.

55. Eventual consistency

A situation in which components can temporarily have different snapshots but converge as updates propagate.

56. Fire-and-forget

Sending a message without awaiting an application-level response before continuing.

57. Request/response

An interaction in which the sender needs a response associated with its request.

58. Handshake / explicit synchronization

A procedure by which a newly initialized subscriber asks for current state rather than relying on events that may have been published before it was listening.

59. Boundary validation

Validating and normalizing data as it crosses a component boundary or trust domain.

Part XIII — Further reading

60. Recommended primary documentation

Chrome Extensions — Message passing

https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/develop/concepts/messaging

Read about runtime.sendMessage(), tabs.sendMessage(), one-time requests, and long-lived connections.

Chrome Extensions — Tabs API

https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/api/tabs

Especially useful for understanding why tabs.sendMessage() accepts a tab ID and can target a particular frame/document.

MDN — runtime.sendMessage()

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Mozilla/Add-ons/WebExtensions/API/runtime/sendMessage

MDN — runtime.onMessage

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Mozilla/Add-ons/WebExtensions/API/runtime/onMessage

Pay attention to sendResponse(), synchronous and asynchronous responses, return true, Promises, and cross-browser compatibility details.

MDN — Window.postMessage()

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/postMessage

Read this alongside the security discussion, especially the origin checks required when communicating between different windows.

Chrome — Execution worlds

https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/api/scripting#type-ExecutionWorld

Connect the messaging patterns in this chapter to the MAIN / ISOLATED distinction from Chapter 1.

61. What have we really learned?

At first glance, this chapter was about APIs such as:

sendMessage()
postMessage()
onMessage

The deeper lesson is that communication becomes part of the architecture when an application is split into contexts with different lifetimes and privileges.

It is no longer sufficient to say "function A calls function B." We must ask:

  • Who produces a message, and who consumes it?
  • Which boundary does it cross?
  • Is a response expected, and can it arrive later?
  • How are updates correlated with their operation?
  • What if a message is delivered twice or out of order?
  • What if the subscriber is not ready yet?

These questions lead naturally into the next chapter.

In Chapter 3, we leave the extension infrastructure and examine one of the least stable environments PlumePilot must work with:

The DOM of a web application we do not control.

Reading an HTML element is easy. Building reliable automation on top of a continuously changing interface is another matter.

← 01 · Anatomy of PlumePilot 03 · DOM and dynamic pages →
Chapter 03

03 — DOM and dynamic pages

Working inside a UI we do not control

In the previous chapter, we followed messages as they crossed the popup, background, bridge, and MAIN world.

Now PlumePilot faces a harder task: understanding a web page built by someone else while that page keeps changing.

We could describe a content script as code that "reads the DOM and clicks elements." Technically true—but not very helpful. The difficult questions are:

  • Does the element already exist, or will it be rendered later?
  • Does the DOM accurately represent the platform's actual state?
  • Is a node saved five seconds ago still part of the current document?
  • Does a closed accordion mean its chapter does not exist, or only that its contents are not rendered?
  • Do two chapters with the same number represent the same chapter?
  • After .click(), when has the action actually taken effect?
  • Do timeouts mean the same thing in a hidden tab?
  • Can an old DOM reference survive a sidebar rebuild?

These are not PlumePilot-specific questions. They arise in extensions, userscripts, end-to-end tests, interactive scrapers, automation, accessibility tools, and integrations with legacy applications.

The central lesson is:

The DOM is a temporary representation of application state, not necessarily the application state itself.

Part I — The DOM is not a database

1. What exactly is the DOM?

When the browser parses HTML, it builds a tree of JavaScript objects.

For example:

<div class="course">
  <div class="chapter">
    <span>1 - Introduzione</span>
  </div>
</div>

can be visualized as:

Document
└── div.course
    └── div.chapter
        └── span
            └── "1 - Introduzione"

JavaScript can traverse and modify that tree:

document.querySelector(".chapter");

The result is an Element representing that particular node at that particular moment.

A modern frontend may do this:

application state changes
         ↓
frontend recalculates UI
         ↓
old nodes are removed
         ↓
new nodes are created

The user may still see "1 - Introduzione", even though JavaScript now faces a different object.

The text is the same. The DOM identity is not.

2. A DOM reference is not a logical identity

Suppose we write:

const row = document.querySelector(".lesson");

Later the platform refreshes its sidebar:

row variable ───────► old, detached node

current DOM ────────► new node representing the same lesson

The variable still holds a valid JavaScript object. It just may not belong to the active document any longer.

This is a stale reference: once valid, now disconnected from the current UI.

DOM identity       ≠       domain identity

"this exact div"   ≠       "this exact lesson"

A lesson is a domain concept. A div is one of its temporary representations.

3. First real example: lessons()

PlumePilot finds lesson rows in content.js:

function lessons() {
  return [...document.querySelectorAll("div.border-t")].filter((x) =>
    x.querySelector(":scope > div.cursor-pointer"),
  );
}

Source: content.js L647–L651.

Notice what the code does not do: it does not cache an initial NodeList globally and reuse it forever, for example:

const allLessons = document.querySelectorAll(...);
``` Each call to `lessons()` queries the **current DOM**. That small choice matters a great deal in a dynamic application.

---

## 4. `querySelectorAll()` returns a static snapshot

`querySelectorAll()` returns a **static**, not live, `NodeList`:

```js
const rows = document.querySelectorAll(".lesson");

If the DOM changes later, the collection does not automatically include the new elements. PlumePilot immediately turns the list into an array:

[...document.querySelectorAll(...)]

Think of it as a snapshot:

t0: DOM = A B C
querySelectorAll() → [A, B, C]

t1: DOM = A D C
old collection     → [A, B, C]
new query          → [A, D, C]

The old collection does not acquire D, and B might have been detached.

Functions such as lessons(), chapters(), and sections() are therefore not merely convenience helpers: they are readers of the current rendered state.

Further reading

MDN documents this non-live behavior: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/querySelectorAll

Part II — Selectors are implicit contracts

5. A CSS selector can become a software dependency

Consider:

document.querySelectorAll("div.border-t");

The .border-t class belongs to the host platform, not to PlumePilot. Our code implicitly assumes:

the platform will continue to render lesson rows
using a structure compatible with this selector

There is no documented versioned API guaranteeing this class will still exist tomorrow. That makes DOM integration inherently more fragile than integration against a stable, versioned contract.

6. Syntactic versus semantic selectors

Compare two approaches.

Strongly structural selector

div > div:nth-child(3) > div:nth-child(2) > span

More semantic selector

[aria-label="lesson-progress"]

The first depends heavily on layout; the second expresses meaning.

Ideally, a host page would provide stable semantic hooks—documented IDs, dedicated data-* attributes, roles, accessible labels, URLs, or domain identifiers.

When we do not control the page, those hooks may be unavailable. PlumePilot has to combine:

CSS classes
relative structure
visible text
URLs
icons
visual state
API data

There is no universally perfect selector. The useful question is:

Which combination of signals is stable enough for the operation we need?

7. :scope reduces ambiguity

lessons() uses:

x.querySelector(":scope > div.cursor-pointer")

In CSS, > means direct child and :scope refers to the element on which the query is being executed.

We are not asking whether any clickable descendant exists somewhere. We are checking for the expected clickable direct child:

row
└── wrapper.cursor-pointer        ✓

versus:

row
└── some unrelated wrapper
    └── nested widget
        └── .cursor-pointer       ✗

The selector encodes a small structural expectation and reduces false positives.

8. closest() recovers an element's context

In Mercatorum chapter identification, PlumePilot uses:

const clickable =
  span.closest("div.cursor-pointer.relative.align-middle") ||
  span.closest("div.cursor-pointer");

Source: content.js L1180–L1198.

closest() starts at a node and walks upward through its ancestors until it finds a match:

clickable div
└── wrapper
    └── span "3 - Title"
         ▲
         └── start here

The meaningful text may be in a span, while the actual interactive component is a parent. This is exactly where closest() helps.

MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/closest

Part III — One domain, multiple DOM structures

9. sections() is already a small cross-platform adapter

A markup structure that seems universal when supporting only Pegaso may stop being universal when adding Mercatorum and San Raffaele. A tempting alternative would be scattered conditions:

if (isMercatorum) ...
else if (isPegaso) ...

These are illustrative branches rather than the adapter interface proposed below.

Consider:

function sections() {
  const nativeSections = pegasoStyleSections();
  if (nativeSections.length) return nativeSections;

  const fallbackChapters = mercatorumChapterRows();
  if (!fallbackChapters.length) return [];

  return [{
    outer: document.documentElement,
    header: null,
    span: fallbackChapters[0].clickable,
    text: MERCATORUM_STATIC_SECTION,
    static: true,
  }];
}

Source: content.js L1201–L1213.

The rest of the algorithm wants to reason about:

sections
  └── chapters
      └── activities

But the host platforms do not expose exactly the same UI hierarchy. Instead of spreading platform-specific conditions throughout the code, sections() returns a common conceptual shape.

The host says, "I render the course like this." PlumePilot translates that into, "For my domain, this is a section."

This is the beginning of a DOM adapter.

10. Normalize first, reason afterward

Backend integrations with multiple providers have the same challenge:

Provider A → customer_id
Provider B → userCode
Provider C → account.id
                 ↓
          { customerId }

An application layer is easier to maintain when it receives one conceptual representation, for example:

{
  customerId: ...
}

Likewise:

Pegaso DOM ────────┐
                   ├──► PlumePilot's conceptual model
Mercatorum DOM ────┘

This separation will return when we discuss how we might structure PlumePilot if we were designing it today.

Part IV — The problem of time

11. document_idle does not mean "application ready"

The manifest loads content.js using:

"run_at": "document_idle"

It is tempting to assume:

content.js starts → page is ready

But document_idle describes extension injection timing, not the readiness of the host application's asynchronous data or UI.

A single-page application may progress through:

initial HTML available
        ↓
content script starts
        ↓
application fetch
        ↓
API response
        ↓
chapters rendered
        ↓
active lesson rendered

At time t0:

chapters().length === 0

At t0 + 800 ms:

chapters().length === 42

Neither observation is necessarily incorrect; they describe different moments.

12. A real regression: initially empty DOM

PlumePilot's changelog preserves a useful case from v2.14.5:

  • The course structure was rendered asynchronously.
  • The "first incomplete activity" algorithm ran before the active lesson row existed.
  • An initially empty DOM was interpreted as a definitive failure.

Historical source: CHANGELOG.md L793–L799.

The critical distinction is:

"not found now"
       ≠
"does not exist"

"not found now" may mean "not rendered yet"

These are semantically different states.

13. The three-state problem

Many DOM bugs originate in treating readiness as a binary decision:

found / not found

The actual states may be:

FOUND
NOT_READY_YET
DEFINITELY_MISSING

An empty chapters() result could mean:

  1. The course truly has no chapters.
  2. We are on the wrong page.
  3. The frontend has not rendered them.
  4. The platform changed its markup and broke our selectors.

We cannot distinguish these cases from the empty array alone. We also need application context and timing.

Part V — Wait for a condition, not an arbitrary number

14. waitFor()

PlumePilot has a deceptively simple central utility:

async function waitFor(fn, timeout = WAIT_MS) {
  let start = Date.now();

  while (Date.now() - start < timeout) {
    const x = fn();

    if (x) {
      return x;
    }

    await sleep(100);
  }

  return null;
}

The real version also accounts for page visibility. The core pattern is shown here.

Source: content.js L1577–L1609.

Instead of:

await sleep(2000);
const chapter = findChapter(...);

we can use:

const chapter = await waitFor(() => findChapter(...));

The conceptual difference is substantial.

15. Fixed delay versus conditional waiting

Fixed delay

wait exactly 2 seconds → try

If the UI is ready in 100 ms, we waste 1.9 seconds. If it is ready after 2.1 seconds, we fail anyway.

Conditional waiting

every 100 ms:
    is the condition true?
        yes → proceed immediately
        no  → retry until timeout

Now the timeout is a deadline, not a guess about how long rendering should take.

16. Polling

waitFor() implements polling: checking a condition repeatedly at a defined interval.

t0       check → false
t0+100   check → false
t0+200   check → true → continue

Polling can seem less elegant than an event, but a system we do not control may not expose any reliable event. Polling can be robust when it is:

  • bounded by a deadline;
  • performed at a sensible interval;
  • driven by a precise condition.

17. When would an event be preferable?

If we owned the host application, it might expose:

courseStore.on("chaptersLoaded", callback);

or:

window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("course-ready"));

PlumePilot does not own such a contract and must infer readiness using observable signals:

DOM / URL / video / API / MutationObserver / polling

This illustrates the difference between software that owns state and software that observes another system's state.

Part VI — MutationObserver: knowing that something changed

18. Why an initial scan is not enough

Toward the end of content.js:

function scan() {
  document.querySelectorAll("video").forEach(attach);
  const activeRow = currentLesson();
  if (activeRow) rememberPlaybackLesson(activeRow);
  scheduleSessionConflictScan();

  if (!courseProgressState || courseProgressState.baselinePercent === null) {
    scheduleCourseProgressInitialization(250);
  }
}

new MutationObserver(scan).observe(document.documentElement, {
  childList: true,
  subtree: true,
});

scan();

Source: content.js L7066–L7090.

The sequence combines an initial scan with observation of later changes. The video we need might not exist when PlumePilot starts.

19. MutationObserver

MutationObserver is a browser API for observing DOM changes.

The configuration:

{
  childList: true,
  subtree: true,
}

means:

childList → detect added and removed children
subtree   → include descendants, not just direct children

The observed target is:

document.documentElement

That is essentially the whole document.

MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MutationObserver

20. Mutation notification is not semantic understanding

An observer can tell us that a node was added. It does not know that the node is "the new video player for lesson 7."

PlumePilot handles this by running:

scan();

rather than attempting to interpret the domain meaning of each mutation record.

DOM mutation notification
          ↓
"something may have changed"
          ↓
recompute the relevant view of state

21. An observer as an invalidation signal

Think of the observer as a cache invalidation signal:

"I know which video elements exist"
          ↓
DOM mutation
          ↓
"that knowledge might be stale"
          ↓
scan()

The notification is not necessarily the new truth. It tells us when we may need to read again.

Part VII — Attaching to elements that appear later

22. document.querySelectorAll("video").forEach(attach)

The scan attaches playback behavior to the currently available video elements:

document.querySelectorAll("video").forEach(attach);

This handles the lifecycle:

PlumePilot starts
    ↓
no <video> exists
    ↓
frontend loads the lesson
    ↓
creates <video>
    ↓
MutationObserver
    ↓
scan()
    ↓
attach(video)

Without later observation, the first scan that found zero videos might also be the last.

23. But a global observer can be expensive

Watching:

document.documentElement

with:

subtree: true

may produce notifications about changes unrelated to autoplay:

tooltips
counters
animations
notifications
menus
unrelated components

Callbacks should therefore be inexpensive, or observations should be coalesced/debounced where appropriate.

PlumePilot's scan is reasonably focused, but the general trade-off remains:

Broad observation is convenient, but increases the number of invalidations we must absorb.

24. Specific versus general observers

Strategy A — Broad observation

observe(document.documentElement, {
  childList: true,
  subtree: true,
});

Advantages: it works no matter where the new component appears, and survives large subtree replacements.

Disadvantages: more notifications; the callback must filter irrelevant changes.

Strategy B — Narrow observation

observe(sidebar, {
  childList: true,
  subtree: true,
});

Advantages: less noise and clearer semantics.

Disadvantages: if the sidebar itself is replaced, we may be watching a detached node; we also need the sidebar to exist before observing it.

On a poorly documented, highly dynamic host page, broad observation can be the pragmatic choice.

Part VIII — A node can disappear while we wait

25. Autoplay and closed accordions

Consider a lesson finishing. PlumePilot must:

1. confirm completion
2. find the current lesson
3. find the next lesson
4. open it

This looks simple until the platform updates the sidebar during the wait, or the user closes an accordion.

The v2.35.1 changelog explicitly describes better recovery with closed accordions, handoff from Objectives, and chapter routing.

Historical source: CHANGELOG.md L3–L10.
