Why not simply take the first entry below 100% and stop?

For a while the algorithm was close to that model. Real experience revealed that the assumption was too strong.

7. Heuristic, index, and source of truth are not synonyms

Suppose the index reports:

Module 1 → 100%
Module 2 → 100%
Module 3 →  80%

It makes sense to inspect module 3 first.

But it does not follow that:

Modules 1 and 2 can never be relevant again

The aggregate data might be slightly stale, updated on a different schedule from detailed endpoints, unable to represent a particular activity state, or temporarily inconsistent with the UI.

Thus:

percentage < 100
       ↓
strong candidate
       ≠
definitive proof

Distinguish:

Source of truth

A source we treat as authoritative for a particular decision.

Index

A structure that helps us quickly find where to search.

Heuristic

A signal that improves search order without independently guaranteeing correctness.

In the current design, the master percentage primarily acts as a prioritization index/heuristic.

Part IV — Candidate ordering

8. The elegant part of the current algorithm

The implementation begins with:

let discoveryOrder = outline
  .map((_entry, index) => index)
  .filter((index) =>
    index >= firstIndex &&
    !(options.verifiedCompleteChapters || []).some((identity) =>
      sameChapterIdentity(outline[index].identity, identity)
    )
  );

It then partitions the candidates:

const suspectedIncomplete = (index) => {
  const route = routeByLessonNumber.get(outline[index].lessonNumber);
  return !route || Number(route.percentage) < 100;
};

 discoveryOrder = [
  ...discoveryOrder.filter(suspectedIncomplete),
  ...discoveryOrder.filter((index) => !suspectedIncomplete(index)),
];

Source: content.js, around lines 5894–5911.

Consider the original order:

[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

with:

1 → 100%
2 → 100%
3 →  80%
4 → 100%
5 →  40%
6 → 100%

The new candidate order is:

[3, 5, 1, 2, 4, 6]

Chapters reported at 100% have not been permanently eliminated. They have been moved to a second pass.

This resembles a stable partition:

suspected incomplete candidates first
other candidates second

while preserving the course order within each group.

Does 80% come before 40% because it has a higher percentage? No. The percentage is not a numeric ranking. We only ask:

suspected incomplete?

and keep the original course order among candidates with the same answer.

That distinction matters because the feature is about finding an incomplete activity in the course's pedagogical sequence, not the activity in the least-complete module.

9. Why not sort by percentage?

It might look natural to write:

chapters.sort((a, b) => a.percentage - b.percentage);

But consider:

Module 3 → 80%
Module 5 → 20%

The first incomplete activity can be in module 3. Sorting by percentage would inspect module 5 before module 3, contrary to the feature's purpose.

The requirement is not:

Find the least-complete chapter.

It is:

Find the first incomplete activity in course order.

The index should reduce the work, not redefine the domain's ordering semantics.

10. Two passes, not an irreversible shortcut

The code explicitly comments:

// Prefer the master's unfinished candidates, keeping course order within
// each pass. A second pass verifies 100% summaries if no candidate matches.

This captures the algorithm's architectural evolution.

An earlier approach might be:

master says 100% → skip forever

That is fast, but a stale master response can cause a false negative:

genuinely incomplete activity
but classified as complete
→ never checked

The safer current approach is:

PASS 1
chapters below 100% or without a reliable mapping

if no valid target is found
         ↓
PASS 2
chapters reported at 100% in the aggregate

The index improves common-case performance while retaining a broader verification path when necessary.

Important nuance: two-pass prioritization protects against permanently overlooking a chapter merely because its summary reads 100%; it does not constitute a mathematical proof of a globally earliest target when different sources disagree. A strict earliest-target guarantee would also require resolving relevant earlier uncertain candidates before committing to a later one.

Part V — Progressive refinement

11. From inexpensive evidence to expensive evidence

We can picture the information sources as a pyramid:

          visual DOM
          highest cost
              ▲
              │
       lesson detail API
              ▲
              │
      course/master index
              ▲
              │
       cache/local state
          lowest cost

The algorithm climbs the pyramid only as needed.

This is progressive refinement:

  1. Consult a coarse, inexpensive representation.
  2. Prioritize plausible candidates.
  3. Request more detailed information.
  4. Use visual verification for remaining uncertainty.

The same pattern appears elsewhere:

database index → row lookup
cache → database
metadata → full file
search index → document retrieval
bounding box → precise collision detection

12. The detail request

For each candidate, PlumePilot can request detailed lesson information:

const lesson = await requestLessonWithRetry(
  courseCode,
  entry.lessonNumber,
  "playback",
  null,
  null,
  lessonLpId,
  false,
  indexedChapter?.id || entry.lessonNumber,
  true,
);

It then examines:

Objectives
videos
progressItems
test

A potential target can be chosen as:

const unfinishedItem =
  !options.forwardVideoSearch && objectivePending
    ? { ...objective, contentType: "intro" }
    : playbackItems.find(
        (item) =>
          item.contentType === "video" &&
          Number(item.percentage) < 100
      );

This is another linear search, but over a much smaller collection: one module's activities.

course index
    ↓
chapter candidate
    ↓
lesson detail
    ↓
activity candidate

13. The result is more than found / not found

A naive helper might return:

return activity || null;

The real workflow needs to distinguish:

target
end
cancelled
fallback

A target result may carry:

{
  status: "target",
  entry,
  unfinishedItem,
  testTarget,
  visualVerification,
  verifiedActivities,
  lessonLpId,
  lessonParagraphId
}

Why so much information?

Because:

we identified the chapter

does not imply:

we know exactly which DOM row to click

The algorithm must communicate both the chosen candidate and how certain the evidence is.

Part VI — Unknown is a real state

14. Three values instead of two

For completion, it is often useful to think in terms of:

complete
incomplete
unknown

rather than a Boolean:

true / false

visibleIncompleteActivity() makes that distinction:

if (percentage === null || !Number.isFinite(percentage)) {
  return { contentType: "unknown", title };
}

Missing information should not automatically become:

0%

because:

I don't know

is different from:

I know it is incomplete

A tempting but dangerous default is:

const percentage = value || 0;

When value is unavailable, this can turn absence of evidence into an apparently exact number.

For critical decisions, unknown must remain representable.

15. False positives and false negatives

Two error categories are especially useful here.

False positive

The algorithm says:

this activity is incomplete

but it is actually complete.

A possible result is an unnecessary navigation or verification.

False negative

The algorithm says:

this activity or chapter may be skipped

but it contains unfinished work.

The result may be a later target or an incorrect "everything completed" conclusion.

For "Find the first incomplete activity", false negatives are generally more costly.

Thus the preferred policy is:

uncertainty → perform an additional check

rather than:

uncertainty → skip permanently

Part VII — When the API is not enough

16. Visual fallback is not algorithm failure

If a lesson response remains incomplete after retries, PlumePilot does not necessarily restart its search:

if (!lesson.ok) {
  return {
    status: "target",
    entry,
    unfinishedItem: null,
    visualVerification: true,
  };
}

Source: content.js, around lines 5979–5995.

The algorithm has already established something valuable:

this is a candidate that cannot be safely ruled out

Instead of:

API failure
→ discard progress
→ restart from chapter 1

it can do:

uncertain API data for module 12
→ open module 12
→ verify visually

This is a targeted fallback.

17. Global versus local fallback

Global

module 12 could not be verified
        ↓
restart at module 1
        ↓
recheck modules 1–11

Local

module 12 could not be verified
        ↓
open module 12
        ↓
verify it

The local version preserves work that has already been completed.

This is a valuable general principle for robust pipelines and distributed systems:

When one stage fails, preserve as much already verified information as possible.

Part VIII — Remember what has already been verified

18. verifiedCompleteChapters

Suppose the visual fallback opens a candidate and discovers that it is actually complete. We should not discard that evidence and start over.

The code preserves a list:

verifiedCompleteChapters: [
  ...(options.verifiedCompleteChapters || []),
  nextIdentity,
]

When building discoveryOrder, already verified chapters are excluded:

!(options.verifiedCompleteChapters || []).some((identity) =>
  sameChapterIdentity(outline[index].identity, identity)
)

This is a small example of negative memoization inside a workflow:

this chapter has already been verified complete
→ do not pay for the same check again

It is not a persistent global cache. It is local memory for the current search.

Part IX — Finding the chapter is not yet navigation

19. Selecting the candidate does not complete the job

Once the algorithm identifies a candidate:

nextIdentity = apiDiscovery.entry.identity;

PlumePilot must turn that logical identity into an action on a live page:

candidate identity
    ↓
openChapter()
    ↓
wait for rendering
    ↓
reacquire current chapter
    ↓
select exact activity

The DOM can change between each step. The implementation therefore waits for the freshly rendered chapter:

let chapterReady = await waitFor(() => {
  const fresh = findChapter(nextIdentity);
  if (!fresh) return null;

  const rows = chapterRows(fresh);
  return rows.length > 0 ? fresh : null;
});

This connects Chapter 08 directly to the dynamic-DOM lessons from Chapter 03. Even a perfect search plan requires careful execution in an asynchronous, changing interface.

20. API evidence versus DOM evidence

During bookmark-style search, PlumePilot chooses how to identify the activity.

When the API has already identified it precisely:

const activity = apiUnfinishedItem || ...;

When more verification is needed:

visibleIncompleteActivity(nextIdentity, apiVerifiedActivities)

The overall information flow is:

API
 ↓
provides evidence
 ↓
DOM
 ↓
confirms or supplements it

Neither source automatically replaces the other. The algorithm combines them according to their strengths.

21. Do not overwrite strong evidence with weak evidence

A real code comment captures this principle:

// Missing sidebar percentages are unknown, not 0%. A verified API
// target must not be replaced by a completed Obiettivi row in the DOM.

When integrating information sources, we need an evidence precedence rule.

For example:

verified API: Video B = 42%
incomplete DOM rendering: percentage unavailable

The missing visual percentage must not be reinterpreted as zero or used to discard the already verified API target.

A weaker signal should not erase stronger evidence merely because it was observed later.

Part X — Tests are a different kind of target

22. Activities do not all have the same semantics

A chapter may contain:

Objectives
videos
Test

The search respects user preferences and the type of activity requiring attention.

A pending test may become the target:

const testNeedsAttention =
  Boolean(test) &&
  (options.bookmarkSearch
    ? pendingTest
    : ...);

Later:

if (activity?.contentType === "test") {
  const test = getEndOfLessonTest(chapterReady);
  ...
  test.scrollIntoView(...);
  return true;
}

So the result is not necessarily:

click a video

It can mean:

bring the user to the test

This is a search across heterogeneous elements that share one abstract property—needing attention—but require different final actions.

Part XI — Concurrency and cancellation

23. A long-running search can become obsolete

At the start of discovery:

smartResumeRunning = true;
const generation = ++smartResumeGeneration;

The code defines:

const isCancelled = () =>
  generation !== smartResumeGeneration ||
  courseCode !== courseCodeFromUrl() ||
  !enabled ||
  busy;

Source: content.js, startFirstIncompleteDiscovery().

The counter is a generation token.

Suppose:

search A starts
    ↓
await API
    ↓
user changes application state
    ↓
search B starts

When A resumes, it must not be allowed to manipulate the page.

Compare:

A's generation

with:

current generation

If they differ:

A is stale
→ stop

This resembles an optimistic-concurrency token: a continuation must prove that it still belongs to the currently authorized operation.

24. Why smartResumeRunning is not enough

A Boolean can answer:

is a search running?

but not:

which search is this callback from?

A generation counter adds temporal identity:

run 17
run 18
run 19

An asynchronous continuation from run 17 cannot accidentally become valid during run 19.

The two mechanisms protect different properties:

Boolean running guard
→ prevents overlapping starts

generation token
→ invalidates continuations from older runs

Part XII — How the algorithm evolved

25. Version 2.14.4 — Smart sequential search

The changelog records an early form of smart resume:

cached outline
→ skip completed chapters/videos
→ consider Objectives
→ find first video below 100%

That was already better than navigating blindly through every activity, but it still depended heavily on detailed sequential checks and the rendered UI.

26. Version 2.14.7 — Course-index-assisted discovery

The course completion index was introduced.

The idea:

aggregate index
→ avoid expensive detail checks for unlikely modules

The changelog describes reusing the index already loaded by the page, skipping modules reported as 100%, checking candidates below 100%, and using visual fallback when detailed verification was unavailable.

This established the architecture:

index → candidate → detail / fallback

27. Version 2.15.0 — From saved preference to one-shot command

The feature also changed its product semantics.

Previously:

Start from the first incomplete activity

was a persistent preference.

It became:

Find the first incomplete activity

an explicit user action.

That change matters algorithmically. The feature is no longer a policy automatically applied at every startup. It becomes:

user query
→ search from the beginning
→ navigate to the result

Essentially, a smart bookmark.

28. Version 2.15.3 — Master-index-first

To reduce work further, the master index became the main tool for choosing a candidate.

Conceptually:

find first percentage below 100%
→ map it to a visible chapter
→ open the precise target

Very efficient—but later observations exposed the risks of treating a summary as definitive.

29. Version 2.35.1 — Prioritize with the index, do not treat it as dogma

The newer algorithm takes a more conservative route:

1. force a master refresh
2. build course outline
3. construct discovery order
4. prioritize chapters below 100%
5. verify candidates
6. inspect chapters reported at 100% if needed
7. use detail APIs
8. use targeted visual fallback when needed

This is the most instructive design.

The optimization remains, but becomes reversible:

heuristic works
→ very fast

If the heuristic fails to identify a valid target:

second pass
→ continue verification

A fast path is useful; preserving an alternative correctness path makes the system more resilient.

Part XIII — Cost analysis

30. Naive cost model

With N chapters:

N DOM openings
N render waits
potentially N detail requests

A rough model is:

T_naive ≈ N × (DOM + render + network)

This is not an exact benchmark; it makes the relative cost sources visible.

31. Index-assisted cost model

Suppose:

N = 40 chapters
K = 3 candidates below 100%

The master index requires approximately one retrieval.

Then:

1 master request
+ up to K detail verifications
+ 1 target DOM opening

In a favorable case:

T ≈ index + K × detail + 1 × DOM

The improvement can be substantial even if building and filtering the arrays remains O(N).

The expensive operations—not the small in-memory loop—have been reduced.

32. Worst case

The unfavorable case might involve a stale master index, candidates below 100% that turn out complete, a second pass over entries reported as 100%, detail requests requiring retries, incomplete responses, and visual verification.

The cost may approach a full scan.

But that is often a desirable property: optimize the common case without deliberately removing the thorough verification path.

Part XIV — The strategy in pseudocode

33. Simplified version of the current strategy

The following is illustrative pseudocode, not a verbatim PlumePilot function:

async function findFirstIncomplete(course) {
  const outline = await getOutline(course);
  const master = await getFreshMasterIndex(course);

  const candidates = partitionStable(
    outline,
    chapter => masterPercentage(chapter) < 100 || !isMapped(chapter)
  );

  const verifiedComplete = new Set();

  for (const chapter of candidates) {
    if (verifiedComplete.has(chapter.id)) continue;

    const detail = await getLessonDetail(chapter);

    if (!detail.isReliable) {
      const visual = await verifyVisually(chapter);

      if (visual.target) return visual.target;

      verifiedComplete.add(chapter.id);
      continue;
    }

    const target = firstIncompleteActivity(detail);

    if (target) return target;
  }

  return null;
}

This does not reproduce every guard, retry, user preference, or navigation detail. It illustrates the separation of outline, index, ordered candidates, detail checks, and local fallback.

Part XV — An information-retrieval problem

34. Precision and recall as a mental model

Without turning PlumePilot into a machine-learning system, we can borrow two concepts from information retrieval.

Precision

Among the candidates we choose to inspect, how many actually contain unfinished work?

Recall

Among all genuinely incomplete chapters, how many does the search avoid missing?

An aggressive index filter might provide:

high precision
low checking cost
but imperfect recall

The second pass over entries reported as 100% improves recall by preserving candidates excluded from the fast path.

In simplified terms:

master-prioritized pass
→ speed

additional verification pass
→ resilience against missed candidates

It is a common trade-off in search systems.

Part XVI — What this algorithm teaches us

35. An index reduces the search space

The index does not have to contain the entire truth.

It may be enough to transform:

40 chapters
    ↓
3 candidates worth checking immediately

This is valuable even when a fallback is still required.

36. Domain order comes before heuristic order

We are not searching for:

the lowest completion percentage

but:

the first incomplete activity

Thus any prioritization strategy must be judged against the pedagogical ordering requirement, not only average speed.

37. Unknown must remain unknown

One of the most dangerous errors in real systems is a silent conversion such as:

missing → false
missing → 0
missing → completed

If the system does not know a value, unknown may be the only honest representation.

38. The best optimizations are reversible

A good optimization says:

try the cheaper path first

not:

delete the more expensive path permanently

Here:

master below 100% → first pass
master at 100%    → second pass when needed

is more resilient than:

master at 100% → never check again

39. Preserve previously verified work

When module 12 cannot be verified:

do not restart at module 1

Open module 12.

If module 12 turns out to be complete:

remember that within the current search

Then continue.

This eliminates redundant checks and keeps fallbacks local.

40. Separate discovery from execution

Discovery answers:

where should I go?

DOM interaction answers:

how do I get there?

These are distinct responsibilities.

They are still intertwined in parts of the existing implementation, but conceptually we could separate them:

Discovery Engine
    ↓
Target
    ↓
Navigation / DOM Adapter

That could be a future architectural evolution, without implying that a refactor is necessary now.

Part XVII — What we might model differently today

41. An explicit DiscoveryCandidate

A model could make information provenance clearer:

type DiscoveryCandidate = {
  chapter: ChapterIdentity;
  lessonNumber: number;
  masterPercentage: number | null;
  confidence: "indexed" | "detailed" | "visual";
  activity?: ActivityIdentity;
  needsVisualVerification: boolean;
};

This would give the candidate an explicit confidence/source field rather than relying on loosely related flags.

42. A result type instead of scattered flags

For example:

type DiscoveryResult =
  | { type: "target"; candidate: DiscoveryCandidate }
  | { type: "end" }
  | { type: "cancelled" }
  | { type: "unavailable"; reason: string };

The current JavaScript already represents something similar implicitly:

status: target
status: end
status: cancelled
status: fallback

The lesson is not "rewrite PlumePilot in TypeScript." It is:

When an algorithm can end in semantically different ways, representing those outcomes explicitly reduces ambiguity.

Part XVIII — Testing the search algorithm

43. The happy path is not enough

A useful test matrix should include at least:

Scenario Master Detail DOM Expected behavior
First module incomplete below 100% valid — Target in module 1
First four complete 100,100,100,100,<100 valid — Target in module 5
Stale master all 100% module 3 incomplete — Module 3 found during second pass
Missing mapping entry without route — valid Targeted visual verification
Incomplete detail below 100% exhausted retries valid Visual verification of candidate
False candidate below 100% complete complete Continue without a full restart
Missing DOM percentage below 100% partial unknown Do not invent 0%
Cancelled search any await in progress — No navigation
Course changes any await in progress — Old run invalidated
Pending test below 100% pending test valid Bring test into view

This kind of matrix often reveals more than line coverage alone, because it tests the relationship between evidence, decisions, and actions.

Part XIX — A backend developer's analogy

Imagine a very large database table:

SELECT *
FROM activities
WHERE completed = false
ORDER BY course_order
LIMIT 1;

Without a useful index, the database may need to examine many rows.

PlumePilot faces a similar problem, but the information is spread across:

master endpoint
lesson endpoint
local cache
DOM

The course index acts like a coarse index. A lesson detail request resembles fetching the complete row. The DOM is like a legacy subsystem we can inspect when structured data is insufficient.

This is not a perfect analogy. There is no full query planner, and PlumePilot does not have a transactionally consistent snapshot across all sources.

But the principle transfers well:

Start with the cheapest representation that meaningfully narrows the search; access expensive detail only for promising candidates.

Part XX — Concepts to carry forward

1. Index and source of truth are different concepts

An index can be tremendously useful even when it is not fully authoritative.

2. Reordering checks is different from eliminating candidates

check chapters below 100% first

is safer than:

never check chapters reported at 100%

3. The important cost is often I/O, not CPU

Avoiding DOM openings and HTTP requests can save far more time than micro-optimizing one JavaScript loop.

4. Unknown is not false

The absence of information must remain representable, rather than being silently converted into a known outcome.

5. The best fallbacks are local

When module 12 cannot be verified, inspect module 12. Do not restart at module 1.

6. Preserve verified evidence

verifiedCompleteChapters avoids repeating checks that already produced trustworthy results.

7. Asynchronous operations must be allowed to become stale

Generation tokens and cancellation guards prevent obsolete searches from acting on the page.

8. Discovery and execution are conceptually distinct responsibilities

discover target
    ↓
navigate to target

is a cleaner model than treating decision-making and DOM manipulation as an inseparable operation.

Part XXI — Exercises

Exercise 1 — Stable partition

Given:

const chapters = [
  { id: 1, percentage: 100 },
  { id: 2, percentage: 75 },
  { id: 3, percentage: 100 },
  { id: 4, percentage: 20 },
];

Produce the order:

[2, 4, 1, 3]

without sorting numerically by percentage. Preserve the relative ordering within both groups.

Exercise 2 — Why can sort() be semantically wrong?

Explain why:

chapters.sort((a, b) => a.percentage - b.percentage);

does not correctly express "first incomplete activity."

Exercise 3 — Three-valued knowledge

Represent progress as:

"complete" | "incomplete" | "unknown"

rather than a Boolean.

Which parts of the algorithm become easier to express?

Exercise 4 — Worst case

Imagine 50 chapters and a master index that incorrectly reports everything at 100%.

How many detailed verifications might be required to preserve thoroughness? Why is this worst-case degradation acceptable?

Exercise 5 — A query planner

Sketch three plans:

DOM-first
API-detail-first
master-index-first

For each, compare the number of requests, number of DOM openings, reliability, and behavior when data is stale.

Part XXII — Further reading

For the JavaScript data operations used directly in this algorithm:

  • MDN — Array.prototype.find()
    https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/find

  • MDN — Array.prototype.filter()
    https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/filter

  • MDN — Map
    https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Map

Studying relational database indexes and query planning will also provide useful analogies. Keep in mind, however, that PlumePilot is not implementing a database management system.

Part XXIII — In the next chapter

We now understand how PlumePilot decides which information to retrieve, and in which order.

Chapter 09 changes the kind of problem completely:

Generating PDF, HTML, and EPUB in the browser.

We will study a pipeline from course structures and resource URLs to downloadable binary files:

collection
    ↓
normalization
    ↓
asset fetching
    ↓
parsing
    ↓
transformation
    ↓
layout / reflow
    ↓
serialization
    ↓
Blob / download

And we will ask a very practical question when the browser processes tens or hundreds of megabytes:

What does it mean to use the browser not merely as a user interface, but as a full document-generation runtime?

Chapter 09

09 — Generating PDF, HTML, and EPUB in the browser

Pipelines, binary data, transformation, and memory

PlumePilot does more than read a web page and automate a few interactions. It also takes information collected from the platform and transforms it into new documents that must be valid, downloadable, and usable outside the browser.

This is an important change of role.

Until now, our systems mostly looked like:

page / API
    ↓
PlumePilot
    ↓
decision / navigation / state

Document generation introduces a different pipeline:

page / API
    ↓
collect data and URLs
    ↓
normalize
    ↓
transform
    ↓
serialize
    ↓
binary or text file
    ↓
local download

It has three main forms:

Course materials → PDF
Course materials → EPUB
Tests            → PDF / offline HTML

Each solves a different problem:

  • PDF mainly preserves the original document faithfully.
  • Offline HTML turns structured data into a small self-contained application.
  • EPUB attempts to reinterpret a fixed-page document as an ebook that adapts to the reader's screen.

The third task is by far the hardest.

Part I — Separate collection from building

1. Two phases that must not be confused

When a user requests course materials, PlumePilot does not immediately generate the file.

First it needs a representation of the materials:

course
  ↓
sections
  ↓
chapters
  ↓
material URLs
  ↓
material[]

Only then can the document-building phase begin.

This separation is architecturally important:

COLLECTION                         BUILD

Multiversity                      builder page
    ↓                                 ↓
content.js                        pdf-core.js
    ↓                             epub-core.mjs
material descriptors                  ↓
    ↓                             final bytes
background.js                         ↓
    ↓                              download
builder job

The collector knows about the course, sections, chapter order, material URLs, and collection failures.

The builder should primarily be concerned with downloading resources, transforming them, laying them out, serializing them, and producing the finished file.

Backend analogy

It resembles:

query / data acquisition
         ↓
normalized DTO
         ↓
report generator

The generator should not need to understand the LMS page's DOM.

2. The builder as a separate process

Chapter 02 showed that the background stores a job payload in chrome.storage.local and opens a dedicated builder page whose URL carries only a small jobId.

Conceptually:

background
   │
   ├── storage["pegasoExportJob:abc123"] = large payload
   │
   └── opens materials-builder.html?job=abc123
                              │
                              ↓
                       builder reads job

This avoids huge URLs and repeatedly serializing large structures in messages.

The builder has its own page with a progress bar, PDF/EPUB buttons, cancellation, error messages, and a lifetime independent of the popup.

The popup can close without necessarily destroying document generation.

Part II — The browser's binary building blocks

3. ArrayBuffer, Uint8Array, and Blob

Ordinary JavaScript application code often deals with strings and objects. PDFs and EPUBs are sequences of bytes.

Three browser types therefore appear throughout the code:

ArrayBuffer
Uint8Array
Blob

For example, pdf-core.js contains:

const bytes = new Uint8Array(await response.arrayBuffer());

The flow is:

HTTP response
     ↓
ArrayBuffer
     ↓
Uint8Array
     ↓
PDF / EPUB library

ArrayBuffer

A raw block of binary memory. By itself, it does not define characters, numbers, or pixels.

Uint8Array

A typed view over unsigned 8-bit values. Each element represents:

0 … 255

It is a natural representation for binary files because their fundamental unit is the byte.

Blob

An immutable binary object that the browser can treat as file-like data. PlumePilot may ultimately produce:

new Blob([bytes], { type: "application/pdf" })

or:

new Blob([bytes], { type: "application/epub+zip" })

The MIME type tells the browser what kind of resource is being produced.

4. From memory to download: Object URLs

A Blob is a JavaScript object. An HTML <a> element expects a URL.

The bridge between them is:

URL.createObjectURL(blob)

The material builder uses this pattern:

function download(bytes, filename, mime) {
  const url = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([bytes], { type: mime }));
  const anchor = document.createElement("a");
  anchor.href = url;
  anchor.download = filename;
  document.body.appendChild(anchor);
  anchor.click();
  anchor.remove();
  setTimeout(() => URL.revokeObjectURL(url), 5000);
}

The browser creates an opaque URL resembling:

blob:chrome-extension://.../uuid

which refers to data managed by the browser:

Uint8Array
    ↓
Blob
    ↓
Object URL
    ↓
<a download>
    ↓
file on the user's computer

Why revokeObjectURL()?

As long as the Object URL remains active, the browser needs to keep the referenced Blob available.

PlumePilot revokes it after a short delay—not immediately—to allow the download to start:

URL.revokeObjectURL(url)

This is a small, concrete example of resource-lifetime management.

Part III — Generating the merged course PDF

5. PDF: compose rather than convert

Generating a combined PDF is conceptually much simpler than generating EPUB.

The source materials are already PDF documents. We do not need to reinterpret their content:

Chapter 1 PDF ─┐
Chapter 2 PDF ─┼──→ combined PDFDocument
Chapter 3 PDF ─┘

The main function in pdf-core.js is:

async function buildCoursePdf(
  courseTitle,
  materials,
  onProgress = () => {},
  fetchImpl = globalThis.fetch,
)

First we create the destination document:

const document = await PDFDocument.create();

Then for each material:

const response = await fetchImpl(material.url);
const bytes = new Uint8Array(await response.arrayBuffer());
const source = await PDFDocument.load(bytes, {
  ignoreEncryption: true,
  updateMetadata: false,
});

We now have two documents:

source   → PDF for one chapter

document → combined PDF being built

6. Copying pages

The core of composition is:

const sourceIndices = source.getPageIndices();
const copiedPages = await document.copyPages(source, sourceIndices);

Then:

for (const copiedPage of copiedPages) {
  const addedPage = document.addPage(copiedPage);
  firstPage ||= addedPage;
}

The algorithm is almost literal:

for each PDF:
    download
    open
    copy every page
    append pages in order

Its enormous advantage is that we are not reconstructing PDF layout.

Equations, graphics, fonts, tables, and page geometry remain those of the source document. The visual-fidelity problem is comparatively small.

7. Adding structure to an existing document

PlumePilot does not merely concatenate pages.

During copying it retains chapter metadata:

included.push({
  chapter: material.chapter,
  chapterTitle: material.chapterTitle,
  section: material.section,
  firstPage,
  pageCount: copiedPages.length,
});

The key property is firstPage.

Once we know each chapter's first page, we can build an interactive contents page, internal links, and PDF bookmarks/outlines:

addInteractiveIndex(document, courseTitle, included, regular, bold);
addBookmarks(document, included);

The pipeline becomes:

original PDFs
     ↓
merge pages
     ↓
chapter → first page mapping
     ↓
contents + bookmarks
     ↓
serialization

8. Serializing the PDF

While manipulating PDFDocument, we have a JavaScript representation of a document.

To produce the actual file:

const bytes = await document.save({
  addDefaultPage: false,
  useObjectStreams: true,
});

Now:

PDFDocument
    ↓ save()
Uint8Array

The remaining step is the Blob-based download discussed earlier.

9. Partial success

One damaged source PDF should not necessarily destroy the entire export.

The loop records both successes and failures:

try {
  ...
  included.push(...);
} catch (error) {
  failures.push(...);
}

The whole operation fails only when no material could be included:

if (!included.length) {
  throw new Error(
    "Non è stato possibile scaricare e unire nessuna dispensa.",
  );
}

The Italian error string is preserved from the historical code snapshot.

This distinguishes:

total failure
vs.
partial success

If 24 of 25 materials are usable, a document containing 24 chapters plus a clear failure report for the remaining one may be much more useful.

Backend analogy

It resembles a batch job collecting:

successes[]
failures[]

rather than enforcing all-or-nothing behavior on work where a partial result has genuine value.

Part IV — Generating the quiz PDF

10. When there are no PDFs to merge

Self-assessment tests are different.

Questions arrive as structured data:

chapter
questions[]
    question
    answers[]
    correctPosition
    images[]

There is no source PDF to concatenate. We must construct the layout.

test-builder.js creates:

const documentPdf = await PDFLib.PDFDocument.create();

It loads bundled Unicode fonts and manually draws titles, questions, answers, images, solutions, internal links, bookmarks, and page numbers.

This pipeline resembles a report renderer.

11. Text layout: the invisible problem

Drawing text in a PDF is not simply:

drawText(longString)

We need to know where each line should end.

The builder's wrap() function measures candidate text using the font:

font.widthOfTextAtSize(candidate, size)

Conceptually:

next word
     ↓
does line exceed width?
  ┌───────┴───────┐
 no              yes
  ↓               ↓
append         end line
               new line

This, too, is an algorithm.

HTML layout is normally handled by the browser. A programmatically generated PDF often makes us responsible for those layout decisions.

12. Images: caching and binary validation

Quiz questions may contain images.

test-builder.js uses:

const imageCache = new Map();

The image loader is:

loadImageAsset(image)

loadImageAsset(image) caches the download Promise itself:

if (imageCache.has(url)) return imageCache.get(url);

const request = (async () => {
  ...
})();

imageCache.set(url, request);
return request;

This is notable: the cache deduplicates concurrent requests, not just completed results.

If two questions request the same image while the first download is still pending:

request A ──────┐
                ├── same Promise
request B ──────┘

There is no second Fetch call.

Validate content, not just file extensions

The builder also checks byte signatures:

const jpeg =
  bytes[0] === 0xff &&
  bytes[1] === 0xd8 &&
  bytes[2] === 0xff;

It recognizes JPEG and PNG signatures rather than trusting an image.jpg suffix or the server's stated MIME type alone.

This is controlled content sniffing. Images are also limited to 8 MiB, helping with both reliability and memory control.

Part V — HTML: turning data into a small application

13. The quiz HTML is not a static document

PlumePilot's generated HTML contains markup, CSS, JavaScript, test data, images, note state, an editor, filters, and answer-checking logic.

It is better understood as:

A self-contained web application distributed in a single file.

The builder exposes:

async function interactiveHtml()

14. Making images work offline

If an HTML export contains:

<img src="https://server.example/image.png">

it does not truly work offline.

The builder therefore downloads each image and converts it to a Data URL:

https://.../image.png
      ↓ fetch
Uint8Array
      ↓ base64
data:image/png;base64,...

The data is embedded directly into the exported file, removing the external dependency.

Trade-off

Base64 makes the file self-contained, but expands binary data in its textual representation.

Roughly:

3 binary bytes → 4 Base64 characters

This generally adds about one third to the encoded payload before other overhead.

It is the familiar trade-off between portability and size.

15. Serializing data inside JavaScript

The builder constructs a JSON payload:

const payload = JSON.stringify({
  courseTitle: job.courseTitle,
  annotatedFilename: ...,
  tests,
})

then applies further escaping:

.replace(/</g, "\\u003c")
.replace(/\u2028/g, "\\u2028")
.replace(/\u2029/g, "\\u2029");

Why?

Because the JSON will be inserted inside a <script> element. Data that is valid JSON may acquire a different meaning when embedded directly into HTML/JavaScript.

The general principle is:

Correct escaping depends on the context into which a value is serialized.

There is no single universal escaping function.

16. Separating runtime from data

The quiz runtime is not manually duplicated inside the builder.

It is loaded from:

const runtimeResponse = await fetch("offline-quiz-runtime.js");
const runtimeSource = await runtimeResponse.text();

Then embedded:

HTML template
   +
CSS
   +
JSON data
   +
offline-quiz-runtime.js
   ↓
interactive-quiz.html

During development, the runtime and the generator remain separate responsibilities. They are combined only in the final exported artifact.

Part VI — EPUB is not a PDF with a different extension

17. What actually is an EPUB?

An EPUB is a ZIP container with a specific structure and contracts.

In simplified form:

book.epub
│
├── mimetype
│
├── META-INF/
│   └── container.xml
│
└── OEBPS/
    ├── package.opf
    ├── nav.xhtml
    ├── toc.ncx
    ├── styles/
    │   └── book.css
    ├── text/
    │   ├── title.xhtml
    │   ├── chapter-001.xhtml
    │   └── ...
    ├── images/
    │   └── ...
    └── fonts/
        └── ...

This structure appears in epub-core.mjs.

The builder creates:

const zip = new globalThis.JSZip();

Then:

zip.file("mimetype", "application/epub+zip", {
  compression: "STORE",
});

The EPUB container specification requires the mimetype file to identify the format and remain uncompressed.

18. container.xml: locating the package document

PlumePilot adds:

META-INF/container.xml

which points to:

OEBPS/package.opf

A reading system can then find the publication's primary package description:

EPUB root
   ↓
container.xml
   ↓
package.opf

19. Manifest and spine

package.opf contains two especially important concepts.

Manifest

Defines which resources belong to the publication:

chapter XHTML
images
CSS
fonts
navigation document

Entries are built in a form such as:

<item
  id="chapter-1"
  href="text/chapter-001.xhtml"
  media-type="application/xhtml+xml"
/>

Spine

Defines the primary reading order:

<itemref idref="title"/>
<itemref idref="nav"/>
<itemref idref="chapter-1"/>
<itemref idref="chapter-2"/>

Thus:

manifest = what resources exist
spine    = in what order they are read

This resembles the distinction between a collection of records and an ordered workflow.

20. Navigation document and contents

PlumePilot also builds:

OEBPS/nav.xhtml

with section and chapter navigation, and keeps a toc.ncx for compatibility with older reading systems.

Each chapter can include a link:

<a href="../nav.xhtml#toc">Torna all'indice</a>

The Italian text is part of the real generated-content example. Internal links are not cosmetic: they make the book navigable.

Part VII — The real problem: PDF → EPUB

21. Fixed layout versus reflow

This is where we reach the central difficulty.

A PDF primarily describes how a page should appear.

A reflowable EPUB primarily describes structured content that the reading system may lay out again.

They are nearly opposite models.

PDF

page 595 × 842

draw text at x=84 y=320
draw a line from A to B
place an image in this rectangle

Reflowable EPUB

<h1>Title</h1>
<p>Paragraph...</p>
<ul>...</ul>

The reader chooses font size, line width, margins, pagination, and orientation.

That makes EPUB comfortable on Kindle and other ereaders—but only when we can reconstruct semantics from a source format that may no longer contain them explicitly.

22. Extracting text is not reconstructing a document

PDF.js can provide a list of text items, but:

"The"
"function"
"f(x)"
"is"
"continuous"

does not tell us automatically which items belong to one paragraph, whether the page contains multiple columns, whether something is a formula, whether a line is a fraction bar, whether an image is essential, or whether a table has lost its row/column relationships.

So conversion is not just:

PDF text → HTML

but:

PDF operators
+ text items
+ coordinates
+ images
+ vector graphics
        ↓
classification
        ↓
preservation strategy

Part VIII — Classifying pages

23. Three strategies, not one

PlumePilot's EPUB converter supports three conceptual modes:

TEXT
VISUAL
REGIONAL / HYBRID

The code records:

const record = {
  chapterIndex,
  pageNumber,
  mode: regional?.html
    ? "regional"
    : visual
      ? "visual"
      : "text",
  ...
};

Text

For pages that can be reliably reconstructed:

PDF text items
      ↓
reconstruct blocks
      ↓
reflowable XHTML

Benefits: selectable text, adjustable fonts, smaller files, better accessibility, and a more natural ebook experience.

Visual

For complex content:

PDF page
   ↓
canvas
   ↓
PNG / JPEG
   ↓
<img>

Benefit: high visual fidelity.

Costs: text is not truly reflowable, files are larger, zoom controls readability, and accessibility is weaker.

Regional

A compromise that separates the page into regions:

┌─────────────────────────┐
│ reflowable text         │
│                         │
├─────────────────────────┤
│ formula / diagram       │ ← image
├─────────────────────────┤
│ reflowable text         │
└─────────────────────────┘

We need not choose between an entirely textual page and one full-page image.

24. pageNeedsVisual() as a classifier

Before converting a page:

const classification = await pageNeedsVisual(page, content);

The function considers significant images, vector graphics, rotated text, parallel columns, tables, suspicious patterns, formulas, and text that cannot be reconstructed safely.

This is a classification heuristic. It does not mathematically prove that a page can be converted. Instead, it chooses the strategy that appears to minimize information loss.

25. Verification after conversion

Even if the initial classifier chooses text, PlumePilot verifies the result:

converted = textPageToHtml(...);

then:

visual = textConversionLooksIncomplete(converted);

The process is:

pre-check
   ↓
conversion
   ↓
post-check

This resembles the progressive refinement from Chapter 08: make a cheap initial decision, then check the actual result.

26. Equations: why they are difficult

A PDF formula might be represented with Unicode, mathematical fonts, individual glyphs, vector lines, images, or combinations of these.

For example:

 a + b
───────
   c

might not be present as one meaningful string: the fraction bar could be an independent drawing command.

PlumePilot looks for cases such as:

hasSimpleFractionRule(...)

and unsupported mathematical characters.

When the risk is high, a rendered region may be more faithful than selectable but mathematically incorrect reconstructed text.

Selectable text is not worth more than correct content.

Part IX — Canvas as a rasterizer

27. From PDF to pixels

For visually preserved pages, PDF.js renders into <canvas>:

PDF page
    ↓
PDF.js render task
    ↓
CanvasRenderingContext2D
    ↓
RGBA pixels

The code calls:

const task = page.render({
  canvasContext: context,
  viewport,
  intent: "print",
});

A canvas is a temporary rendering surface.

28. From canvas to image

encodeCanvas() chooses PNG or JPEG and calls:

canvas.toBlob(...)

then:

new Uint8Array(await blob.arrayBuffer())

The data flow is:

canvas pixels
     ↓
toBlob()
     ↓
PNG/JPEG Blob
     ↓
ArrayBuffer
     ↓
Uint8Array
     ↓
EPUB asset

29. PNG or JPEG?

No format is universally better.

JPEG often compresses photographic material more efficiently. PNG can preserve rasterized text, diagrams, sharp lines, and images with limited colors better.

chooseCanvasFormat() samples the content to choose between strategies.

This is another adaptive decision based on data.

Part X — Memory as an architectural constraint

30. Why EPUB can consume a lot of RAM

The final file size does not equal the memory required to construct it.

A rasterized page with:

2000 × 2800 pixels

requires approximately:

2000 × 2800 × 4 bytes
= 22,400,000 bytes
≈ 21.4 MiB

for an uncompressed RGBA buffer, even if its PNG encoding occupies only a few megabytes.

Several representations may coexist:

PDF bytes
PDF.js structures
text items
operator list
RGBA canvas
encoded image bytes
JSZip entries
final ZIP buffer

Therefore an 80 MB EPUB does not imply an 80 MB peak-memory footprint. Its working set can be considerably larger.

31. Peak memory, not total allocation

The key question is not just "How many bytes do we allocate in total?" It is:

How many bytes remain live simultaneously at the worst point?

This is peak memory.

Compare:

Strategy A

load 100 pages
render 100 canvases
retain everything
create ZIP

with:

Strategy B

load chapter
  page 1 → convert → release
  page 2 → convert → release
  ...
clean up PDF
next chapter

Both may do similar total work. Strategy B keeps fewer large objects alive simultaneously.

PlumePilot attempts to follow the second strategy.

32. page.cleanup()

The code uses:

finally {
  page.cleanup();
}

finally is important: even after conversion failure, we want PDF.js to release resources belonging to the page.

success ─┐
         ├──→ cleanup
error ───┘

This is exactly the resource-lifetime principle studied in Chapter 05.

33. Shrinking canvas dimensions to 1 × 1

Several paths end with:

canvas.width = 1;
canvas.height = 1;

A canvas can retain a large backing buffer. Resizing it encourages the browser to replace that surface with an almost empty one:

2000 × 2800 canvas
      ↓
no longer needed
      ↓
1 × 1 canvas

This is not a direct call to the garbage collector. JavaScript does not provide a general:

free(canvasMemory);

But we can release references and reduce native resources that objects retain.

34. Destroying the PDF.js document

At the end of convertMaterial():

if (pdf) {
  await pdf.destroy().catch(() => {});
} else if (loadingTask) {
  await loadingTask.destroy().catch(() => {});
}

PDF.js can retain caches, worker state, fonts, operator lists, pages, and streams. We want the lifetime:

convertMaterial(chapter)
    ↓
PDFDocumentProxy alive
    ↓
convert all pages
    ↓
destroy()
    ↓
next chapter

35. Yielding to the browser

After each page:

await yieldToBrowser(signal);

This does not necessarily reduce overall work. It lets the browser update the UI, process events, respond to cancellation, and render progress smoothly.

This is cooperative scheduling.

Part XI — Asset deduplication

36. Identical content may appear multiple times

Visual conversion can produce repeated images:

image A → 1 MB
image A → 1 MB
image A → 1 MB

Without deduplication, these copies occupy 3 MB.

epub-assets.mjs defines:

const byHash = new Map();

37. Content-addressable deduplication

For each image, the code computes:

const digest = new Uint8Array(
  await crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", image.bytes)
);

and a key:

const key = `${image.mediaType}:${extension}:${hash}`;

The conceptual flow is:

image bytes
     ↓ SHA-256
hash
     ↓
Map lookup
  ┌──┴───┐
 hit    miss
  │       │
reuse   zip.file()

This is a miniature form of content-addressable storage.

The identity is determined by content, not the original filename.

38. Why not keep two copies of the bytes?

A useful comment in epub-assets.mjs says:

// Export-scoped: hold only metadata here. JSZip owns unique encoded buffers.

The Map primarily holds metadata:

{
  name,
  mediaType,
  size,
}

The unique bytes are entrusted to JSZip.

After registration, epub-core.mjs also does:

image.bytes = null;

for registered images.

Deduplicating the output matters; avoiding duplicate live buffers is even more important for memory.

Part XII — Packaging and compression

39. JSZip as an in-memory build system

As chapters are converted, the code adds resources:

zip.file(...)

JSZip behaves like a virtual filesystem:

zip
├── mimetype
├── META-INF/container.xml
└── OEBPS/...

Finally it serializes that structure:

const bytes = await zip.generateAsync({
  type: "uint8array",
  compression: "DEFLATE",
  compressionOptions: { level: 6 },
});

The result is one Uint8Array.

40. The hardest phase to cancel

Immediately before compression, PlumePilot reports:

cancellable: false

to disable the Cancel button.

Until that stage, the code frequently checks:

throwIfAborted(signal);

or uses cancellable operations.

During JSZip.generateAsync() it cannot offer the same control over work already started.

Therefore the UI makes an honest promise:

conversion → cancellable
final compression → finalizing; wait

An interface should not advertise a capability the underlying implementation cannot reliably deliver.

Part XIII — End-to-end cancellation

41. AbortController in the builder

When an EPUB build begins:

buildController = new AbortController();

The signal is passed to:

buildCourseEpub(..., {
  signal: buildController.signal,
});

The Cancel button calls:

buildController.abort();

The signal crosses the entire pipeline.

42. Cancelling a download

fetchPdfWithRetry() creates a local controller for each attempt:

const controller = new AbortController();

and connects the external abort:

const cancel = () => controller.abort();
signal?.addEventListener("abort", cancel, { once: true });

Two distinct causes are handled:

user clicks Cancel
        │
        ├────────────┐
        │            ↓
        │         fetch abort
        │
        └────→ pipeline abort

or

download timeout
        ↓
local controller abort

User cancellation and timeout are not identical, even if both may interrupt Fetch.

43. Cancelling PDF.js

Rendering must respond too.

renderPage() registers:

const cancel = () => task.cancel();
signal?.addEventListener("abort", cancel, { once: true });

convertMaterial() also destroys its active document.

Cancellation is not merely:

set cancelled = true

It propagates to the expensive work itself. This is a cancellation pipeline.

Part XIV — Retry and resilience

44. Selective retry

The PDF downloader defines:

const PDF_DOWNLOAD_RETRY_DELAYS_MS = [1000, 2500];

But not every failure triggers retry.

Client errors:

status >= 400 && status < 500

are treated differently, with exceptions for potentially transient codes such as:

408 Request Timeout
429 Too Many Requests

Retrying a 404 soon afterward is unlikely to help. Timeouts, unstable networks, and rate limiting may justify a further attempt.

As in Chapter 04, retry is not indiscriminate repetition.

45. Invalidating failed links

If generation discovers that a cached material URL is unusable, the builder reports:

PEGASO_INVALIDATE_MATERIAL_CACHE

with the relevant failed cacheKeys.

The feedback loop is:

collector
   ↓
cache material URL
   ↓
builder tries URL
   ↓
download fails
   ↓
invalidate cache

A cache's consumer helps correct the cache.

Part XV — References and ownership

46. Garbage collection does not mean perfect automatic resource management

JavaScript uses garbage collection, but that does not mean memory can be ignored.

The collector can reclaim an object only once it becomes unreachable. References inside Maps, arrays, closures, JSZip, event listeners, and Object URLs may keep objects alive.

Some browser APIs also own native resources whose lifetimes do not map neatly onto the JavaScript object alone.

That is why PlumePilot uses explicit operations such as:

page.cleanup()
pdf.destroy()
canvas.width = 1
image.bytes = null
URL.revokeObjectURL()
removeEventListener()

The principle is:

Garbage collection reclaims unreachable memory; architecture must avoid keeping unnecessary objects and resources reachable.

47. Ownership

When handling large binary objects, ask:

Who owns these bytes now?

During image deduplication:

renderRegionalPage
      ↓
image.bytes
      ↓
assetRegistry.register()
      ↓
JSZip owns the unique required buffer
      ↓
image.bytes = null

Thinking about ownership helps even in JavaScript, which does not have Rust's borrow checker.

Part XVI — Comparing the three pipelines

48. PDF, HTML, and EPUB

Property Materials PDF Quiz HTML Materials EPUB
Main input Original PDFs Structured JSON Original PDFs
Transformation Copy pages Web rendering PDF interpretation
Visual fidelity Very high Native HTML Adaptive
Reflow No Yes Yes / hybrid
Interactivity Limited High Reader-dependent
Offline Yes Yes Yes
Conversion complexity Relatively low Medium High
Memory pressure Medium Low/medium High
Binary assets PDFs Inline images ZIP images/fonts

The single word export actually hides three different architectures.

49. Lossless versus lossy transformation

Merging PDFs is close to a lossless visual transformation:

PDF → copy pages → PDF

EPUB conversion necessarily carries greater potential for lossy transformation:

PDF visual layout
      ↓ interpretation
semantic XHTML

That is why PlumePilot uses visual fallbacks.

There are two competing goals:

reflowability
     ↑
     │
     │ trade-off
     │
     ↓
fidelity

Regional mode searches for a useful middle ground.

Part XVII — The pipeline as a transformation graph

50. Think in stages

A useful representation of EPUB generation is:

This is closer to a compiler pipeline than a typical UI function.

Each stage accepts one representation, produces another, may fail, and has its own memory costs.

51. Intermediate representation

Compiler design often uses an IR — intermediate representation.

There is a similar pattern here:

PDF operators
      ↓
classification
      ↓
converted.html + images[]
      ↓
EPUB chapter XHTML + assets

converted effectively acts as an intermediate representation: no longer the original PDF, not yet packaged as EPUB.

The architectural insight:

As a transformation grows more complex, explicit intermediate representations improve testability and separation of responsibilities.

Part XVIII — Observability and diagnostics

52. Progress is more than UX

The builder receives callbacks like:

onProgress({
  completed,
  total,
  percent,
  message,
  details,
});

This powers the progress bar, but also exposes pipeline stages:

download
conversion
page X of Y
compression

That helps debugging. If a user reports:

"It always gets stuck at page 42 of material 7."

we have more actionable information than:

Building...

53. Structured diagnostics

epub-core.mjs also accepts a diagnostics object that can record information such as:

page mode
classification reason
imageCount
imageBytes
mathFontBytes
epubBytes
elapsedMs

This is instrumentation separated from primary behavior. Collecting diagnostics should not change the conversion result.

Part XIX — Possible future directions

54. Streaming

The current implementation constructs an EPUB in memory with JSZip and eventually produces a single Uint8Array.

Very large documents might benefit from a more streaming-oriented design:

input chapter
    ↓
convert
    ↓
append to archive
    ↓
release intermediates

with an archive writer that does not retain the complete file in memory.

That would be more complex and depend on available browser APIs and libraries. It is not automatically a better choice for typical documents.

55. Dedicated workers

Some expensive transformations could theoretically run away from the main thread:

builder UI
    ↓ message
Web Worker
    ↓
conversion / encoding

But transferring work is not free:

  • The ordinary DOM is main-thread-only.
  • Canvas use may require different APIs such as OffscreenCanvas.
  • Libraries have their own constraints.
  • Passing large buffers needs careful design.
  • Debugging and cross-browser support become more complex.

"Put it in a worker" is not a universal solution.

56. Backpressure

When one pipeline stage produces data faster than the next can consume it, memory can accumulate. This is backpressure.

A problematic design:

render 200 pages quickly
        ↓
images[] grows
        ↓
ZIP processes data more slowly

Converting sequentially by page or chapter naturally reduces this risk.

It is another reason why maximum concurrency is not necessarily the fastest or safest strategy.

Part XX — Error model

57. Not all errors are the same

Document generation can encounter:

network error
HTTP error
invalid PDF
empty PDF
unsupported image
conversion uncertainty
render failure
timeout
user cancellation
archive failure

These demand different handling.

Retry

For potentially temporary failures.

Fallback

For content whose semantics cannot be reconstructed reliably but whose visual appearance can still be preserved.

Skip and report

For one unusable chapter, when the remaining export is still valuable.

Abort the whole operation

When the user cancels, no chapter can be produced, or integrity of the final artifact cannot be guaranteed.

This taxonomy is more useful than a generic:

catch (error) {
  alert("Errore");
}

which discards essential information. The Italian string is preserved from the source example.

Part XXI — Backend analogy

58. Document generation as ETL

A useful analogy is an ETL pipeline:

Extract
  ↓
Transform
  ↓
Load

For PlumePilot:

Extract
→ URLs / APIs / PDF bytes

Transform
→ pages / XHTML / images / metadata

Load
→ PDFDocument or EPUB ZIP

There is an important difference. A backend server often has substantially more memory, temporary filesystems, separate processes, job queues, and flexible streaming.

The browser has a more constrained runtime and shares resources with the user's interface.

That makes working-set management a visible part of the architecture.

Part XXII — Testability

59. Pure functions are valuable

epub-core.mjs exposes some helpers through:

export const __testing = {
  cleanExtractedText,
  chapterLabelFor,
  estimateBodySize,
  ...
  pageNeedsVisual,
  textConversionLooksIncomplete,
  textPageToHtml,
  ...
};

This allows decisions to be tested separately:

Should this page use visual mode?
Do these text items represent columns?
Does this extracted text look suspicious?

without building a complete EPUB for every test.

A useful pattern is:

external I/O
     ↓
pure or mostly pure functions
     ↓
final I/O

The more logic we can isolate in that testable middle, the easier the system is to reason about.

60. Golden files

Document generators can also use golden files as test fixtures:

input fixture PDF
      ↓
conversion
      ↓
expected artifact

Tests may compare ZIP structure, manifest, chapter count, selected page modes, images, links, extracted text, and size within reasonable ranges.

Exact byte-for-byte output comparisons are not always appropriate, because UUIDs, timestamps, and compression details can differ.

Comparing the artifact's semantics is often more robust.

Part XXIII — Exercises

61. Exercise 1 — Calculate the working set

Imagine three canvases, each:

1800 × 2400

pixels, with RGBA backing buffers.

How much memory do they occupy simultaneously?

width × height × 4 × canvasCount

The purpose is not only the arithmetic. Also ask:

Could we avoid keeping all three canvases alive at the same time?

62. Exercise 2 — Offline HTML

Imagine an offline quiz with 100 images, each 500 KiB.

If all images are embedded as Base64:

  • Approximately how large might the payload become?
  • Is a single HTML file still preferable?
  • At what point would a ZIP containing separate files make more sense?

There is no universal threshold. This is a product decision as much as an engineering decision.

63. Exercise 3 — Fidelity policy

Consider three pages:

A. paragraphs only
B. text with a complex equation
C. a mostly graphical slide

Which preservation strategy would you choose?

Probably:

A → text
B → regional
C → visual

Now ask:

Which observable signals would allow an algorithm to choose automatically?

That is exactly the problem addressed by pageNeedsVisual().

64. Exercise 4 — Partial success

A course contains 30 material PDFs. Number 17 returns HTTP 404.

Which behavior do you prefer?

A. Fail everything
B. Build 29 chapters and report the failure of chapter 17
C. Retry forever
D. Silently replace chapter 17 with a blank page

For PlumePilot's domain, B is generally the most useful.

That would not necessarily hold for a digital signature or database transaction log, where completeness requirements can be very different.

Part XXIV — Concepts to carry forward

65. Main lessons

1. An export is a pipeline

Not one function that "creates a file":

collection → normalization → transformation → packaging → download

2. Data representations change throughout the pipeline

URL
→ Response
→ ArrayBuffer
→ Uint8Array
→ PDF model / canvas / XHTML
→ archive
→ Blob

3. PDF and EPUB solve different problems

PDF prioritizes geometry and fixed-page fidelity.

Reflowable EPUB prioritizes structure and adaptability.

Converting between them requires interpretation.

4. Visual fallback protects correctness

When semantic conversion becomes uncertain, an image can be more faithful than poorly reconstructed text.

5. Memory depends on simultaneously live objects

Output size is only one part of the problem.

6. Cleanup and ownership matter even in JavaScript

Garbage collection does not remove the need to manage lifetimes, listeners, Object URLs, canvases, and resources retained by libraries, native code, or workers.

7. Content-based deduplication reduces file and working-set size

A content hash can identify truly identical assets regardless of filename.

8. Cancellation must propagate through the pipeline

A Cancel button is useful only if expensive stages receive and honor its signal.

9. Partial success is a domain decision

Not every batch must be atomic.

10. Complex transformations benefit from representation boundaries

As a system grows, explicitly defining stages and intermediate structures improves its design.

Part XXV — Chapter glossary

Important terms introduced or expanded upon:

  • ArrayBuffer
  • Uint8Array
  • Blob
  • Object URL
  • MIME type
  • Serialization
  • Rasterization
  • Reflow
  • Fixed layout
  • Lossless / lossy transformation
  • Intermediate representation
  • Content-addressable storage
  • Deduplication
  • Working set
  • Peak memory
  • Ownership
  • Backpressure
  • Cooperative scheduling
  • Partial success
  • Golden file

Toward Chapter 10

The offline HTML quiz showed us something new.

We are no longer just generating a file. We are generating an application that the user can edit.

Inside that small application, PlumePilot needs to manage the cursor, text selection, formatting, lists, checklists, callouts, colors, question statuses, and note storage.

This leads to the next problem:

How do you build a small rich-text editor using the browser's DOM, without relying on a complete editing framework?

In Chapter 10 — A small rich-text editor, we will explore contenteditable, Selection, Range, formatting commands, nested lists, and the details that make a seemingly small editor surprisingly difficult to implement reliably.

← 08 · First incomplete activity 10 · A small rich-text editor →
Chapter 10

10 — A small rich-text editor

contenteditable, Selection, Range, lists, and callouts

In Chapter 09, we saw that the HTML quiz generated by PlumePilot is not simply a document: it is a small offline application.

With version 2.35.0, that application gained another interesting feature: two note fields for each question—Explanation and Observations—became small rich-text editors instead of plain text boxes.

Users can apply bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, superscript and subscript; create bulleted and numbered lists, checklists, colored highlights, and callouts; hide text for review; insert mathematical symbols; undo and redo; use keyboard shortcuts; and mark the personal review status of a question.

At first this might look like a formatting problem:

user presses B
    ↓
make text bold

But a rich-text editor must constantly answer harder questions:

Where is the caret?
What is selected?
Does the selection still belong to this editor?
Did a toolbar click destroy the selection?
Are we inside a list, checklist, or callout?
Does highlighted text already have another color?
What should pressing Enter do?
Where should typing resume after Escape?
How do we persist HTML without allowing arbitrary markup?
How do we recreate the editor after a rerender?

Using offline-quiz-runtime.js as a case study, this chapter explains a fundamental idea:

A rich-text editor does not merely change a string. It changes a DOM tree, a selection, an editing state, and a persistable representation at the same time.

Part I — From textarea to contenteditable

1. Why a textarea is not enough

A normal <textarea> essentially stores a string:

"This is my explanation"

We can easily inspect:

textarea.value
textarea.selectionStart
textarea.selectionEnd

But the text has no HTML structure. We cannot naturally represent:

<strong>this part</strong>
<ul>
  <li>point one</li>
  <li>point two</li>
</ul>

without inventing a custom format or exposing markup to the user.

With contenteditable, an ordinary DOM element becomes editable:

const editor = document.createElement("div");
editor.contentEditable = "true";

PlumePilot creates two editors for each question:

const editor = document.createElement("div");
editor.className = "note-editor";
editor.contentEditable = "true";
editor.setAttribute("role", "textbox");
editor.setAttribute("aria-label", labelText);
editor.setAttribute("aria-multiline", "true");

Historical reference:

offline-quiz-runtime.js:470–490

The conceptual difference is enormous. In a textarea, the primary state is a string. In a contenteditable element, the visible content becomes a tree:

editor
├── text
├── <strong>
│      └── text
├── <span class="highlight">
│      └── text
├── <ul class="checklist">
│      ├── <li>
│      └── <li>
└── <div class="callout">
       └── text

This immediately introduces the concept of a document model.

2. contenteditable is not a complete editor

Writing:

<div contenteditable="true"></div>

does not mean we have built an editor. It only delegates some editing operations to the browser: inserting and deleting text, moving the caret, selecting content, keyboard composition, some paragraph/list management, and interaction with the browser's input system.

The browser also chooses many details of the generated DOM.

For instance, pressing Enter is not semantically equivalent to:

editor.innerHTML += "<br>";

The result depends on whether the caret is inside a paragraph, list, list item, callout, inline node, or empty editor.

contenteditable provides an editing host, not a high-level data model.

PlumePilot must build its own editing protocol on top of that behavior.

Part II — Selection and Range

3. The caret is a collapsed selection

When we say "the caret is after this word," the browser represents that position through the Selection API.

PlumePilot reads it with:

const selection = window.getSelection();

A Selection describes what the user has selected in the document. It may be non-collapsed:

"this [part of the text] matters"

or collapsed:

"this part| of the text"
          ↑
         caret

The caret is not an entirely separate concept. It is essentially a selection whose beginning and end coincide.

4. What is a Range?

A Selection contains one or more Range objects. For our ordinary editing case, think of a range as four coordinates:

startContainer
startOffset
endContainer
endOffset

Consider:

<p>The answer is important.</p>

If we select answer, a range describes two positions inside the DOM tree—not necessarily a pair of string indices.

This matters because a selection can cross multiple nodes:

<p>
  The <strong>answer</strong> is <em>very important</em>.
</p>

Rich-text editing requires reasoning about tree positions, not just character positions.

5. Why PlumePilot saves selectedRange

The runtime declares:

let activeField = null;
let selectedRange = null;

and:

const rememberSelection = () => {
  const selection = window.getSelection();
  if (
    activeField &&
    selection.rangeCount &&
    activeField.contains(selection.anchorNode) &&
    activeField.contains(selection.focusNode)
  ) {
    selectedRange = selection.getRangeAt(0).cloneRange();
  }
};

Historical reference:

offline-quiz-runtime.js:246–252

Why clone the range? Imagine:

1. Select "correct answer".
2. The selection belongs to the editor.
3. Click the "Yellow" toolbar button.
4. The button receives the interaction.
5. The browser may move focus or selection.
6. The click handler may no longer find the original selection.

Relying only on:

window.getSelection()

during the click would be unsafe.

Instead, the editor records:

selection.getRangeAt(0).cloneRange()

as a snapshot of the editing position.

6. Why toolbar buttons intercept mousedown

The toolbar builder uses:

item.addEventListener("mousedown", (event) => event.preventDefault());

Historical reference:

offline-quiz-runtime.js:391–409

This tiny detail matters: by default, interacting with a button can move focus to it.

The desired flow is:

selection inside editor
       ↓
toolbar click
       ↓
preserve editing context
       ↓
apply transformation to previous selection

PlumePilot uses two complementary protections:

preventDefault on mousedown
+
cloned selectedRange

This is defensive UI programming: when correctness depends on a selection, do not rely on one incidental browser behavior.

7. Restoring a selection

Before running a command, runCommand() does:

editor.focus();

if (selectedRange && editor.contains(selectedRange.commonAncestorContainer)) {
  const selection = window.getSelection();
  selection.removeAllRanges();
  selection.addRange(selectedRange);
}

then:

document.execCommand(command, false, value);

Historical reference:

offline-quiz-runtime.js:253–263

The flow is:

saved Range
    ↓
focus editor
    ↓
remove current ranges
    ↓
restore saved Range
    ↓
execute command

It resembles a small editing transaction.

Part III — Native commands and custom transformations

8. PlumePilot's hybrid strategy

The runtime uses two families of operations.

Browser-managed operations

bold
italic
underline
strikeThrough
insertUnorderedList
insertOrderedList
superscript
subscript
undo
redo
removeFormat
insertText

through:

document.execCommand(...)

Custom DOM operations

colored highlights
study mask
checklist semantics
callouts
controlled callout exit
list normalization
sanitization

This distinction is instructive. PlumePilot does not attempt to rebuild the browser's entire editing engine, but native commands are also not sufficient for its custom semantics.

9. execCommand() and deliberate technical debt

document.execCommand() is now a deprecated API, not part of a modern, stable Web editing standard. We should acknowledge that explicitly.

Why use it anyway? For a small offline editor, it offers practical advantages:

  • The browser handles complex operations such as bold, lists, and undo.
  • It integrates with ordinary contenteditable editing.
  • Many changes participate in the browser's native undo history.

The final advantage is particularly difficult to reproduce correctly through direct DOM mutations.

The rationale is not:

execCommand is the recommended modern API

It is:

small feature scope
+ verified compatibility with target browsers
+ value of native undo behavior
+ much higher cost of a complete custom editor
------------------------------------------------
pragmatic use of a legacy API

Legacy does not automatically mean broken, but it does imply risks: browser differences, an uncertain future, unpredictable interactions with input/beforeinput, and potential differences between native and custom DOM editing.

Backend analogy

This resembles using a stable legacy dependency in a narrowly scoped service. The useful questions are not merely "Is it old?" but "How much would replacement cost, what guarantees do we need, and how well can we isolate it?"

PlumePilot keeps this dependency relatively contained within the offline quiz runtime.

Part IV — Range as a transformation tool

10. Highlighting is more than changing CSS

PlumePilot implements highlights with a semantic wrapper rather than execCommand():

<span class="highlight" data-color="yellow">
  text
</span>

The main helper is:

wrapSelection(editor, className, key, value)

Historical reference:

offline-quiz-runtime.js:343–390

It first checks for a useful selection:

if (
  !selectedRange ||
  selectedRange.collapsed ||
  !editor.contains(selectedRange.commonAncestorContainer)
) return;

An empty selection is not interpreted arbitrarily.

11. A structural guard: do not cross incompatible blocks

The code contains:

if (
  range.startContainer.parentElement?.closest("div,li,p") !==
  range.endContainer.parentElement?.closest("div,li,p")
) return;

PlumePilot rejects a custom wrapper when the selection crosses different blocks.

Wrapping:

<p>first half...</p>
<ul>
  <li>...second half</li>
</ul>

inside one <span> could produce invalid or surprising structure.

This is a structural guard:

selection inside one compatible block
        ↓
allow operation

selection crosses incompatible blocks
        ↓
fail safely

It repeats a principle from autoplay and reverse engineering: if we cannot safely preserve structure, do not invent a transformation.

12. extractContents() + insertNode()

The main transformation uses:

const contents = range.extractContents();
wrapper.appendChild(contents);
range.insertNode(wrapper);

Consider:

DOM before

<p>
  abc [def ghi] lmn
</p>

extractContents() moves the selected part into a DocumentFragment:

DocumentFragment
└── "def ghi"

Then:

wrapper.appendChild(contents);

produces:

<span class="highlight" data-color="yellow">
  def ghi
</span>

And:

range.insertNode(wrapper);

inserts it back at the correct position:

<p>
  abc
  <span class="highlight" data-color="yellow">def ghi</span>
  lmn
</p>

This is real structural DOM manipulation with Range.

13. Changing an existing highlight's color

Suppose the editor contains:

<span class="highlight" data-color="yellow">
  important concept
</span>

The user selects all its text and applies blue.

PlumePilot recognizes:

if (
  startHighlight &&
  startHighlight === endHighlight &&
  editor.contains(startHighlight) &&
  range.toString() === startHighlight.textContent
) {
  startHighlight.dataset.color = value;
  ...
}

Instead of nesting another highlight:

<span class="highlight" data-color="yellow">
  <span class="highlight" data-color="blue">
    important concept
  </span>
</span>

it updates the existing node. This prevents unnecessary markup nesting.

14. Changing only part of an existing highlight

A harder case starts with:

[yellow: abc DEF ghi]

Select only DEF and make it blue. The desired result is:

[yellow: abc ]
[blue: DEF]
[yellow:  ghi]

not a blue wrapper nested inside yellow.

The code checks whether the new wrapper ended up within an older highlight:

const oldParent = wrapper.parentElement;

if (className === "highlight" && oldParent?.classList.contains("highlight")) {
  const before = oldParent.cloneNode(false);
  const after = oldParent.cloneNode(false);
  ...
}

Then it reconstructs three segments:

before
new wrapper
after

Here we clearly see that a rich-text editor is a tree-rewriting system.

Part V — Formatting state and the caret

15. Active formatting versus formatted text

One of the hardest problems is distinguishing formatting already attached to text from formatting that will be applied to the next typed character.

For example:

H₂O|

If the caret remains inside <sub>, subsequent characters may also be subscript.

Similarly:

[yellow highlight: important|]

the browser may continue inserting characters inside the highlight span.

But the user's intention may be: "I'm done with this formatting; I want to continue normally."

This motivated the Escape shortcut.

16. Escape as an editing-state reset

The key handler checks:

if (event.key === "Escape") {

Historical reference:

offline-quiz-runtime.js:511–545

When a non-collapsed selection exists:

if (!range.collapsed) selection.collapseToEnd();

The formatted text remains, but the caret moves to the end.
